One prisoner screamed and raged and was released early. Christina Maslach, a young psychologist who had just finished her doctorate, visited, was horrified, and challenged Zimbardo. The study, planned for two weeks, ended after six days. Decades later, released tapes and interviews changed the picture. In one recording, the warden urges a reluctant guard to be tougher. The prisoner who broke down later said he had partly been acting so he could leave. Several guards said they were performing the role they thought was wanted.
study.finding: The original report described rapid abuse by guards and distress in prisoners. Later evidence suggests that guards were encouraged to be harsh, so the result cannot show that roles alone produce cruelty.

entries.statusNote: As a scientific test, the study has collapsed. It was never repeated in its original form, and the researchers shaped what happened. In 2002, the BBC Prison Study by Alex Haslam and Stephen Reicher set up a similar prison without coaching the guards. The guards did not spontaneously become tyrants, and group dynamics went in a very different direction. In 2018 and 2019, Thibault Le Texier used the archives to document the coaching and staging. A small study also suggested that an advert mentioning 'prison life' attracts more aggressive volunteers. What survives is a weaker point: leaders and expectations can push people towards cruelty.
life: When you hear 'anyone would do this in that situation', ask who set the expectations. Leaders who reward harshness usually get more of it.
In any role with power over others, write down what good conduct looks like. Clear norms counter the drift towards abuse.
Be wary of famous studies told as gripping stories. Check whether they were ever repeated before treating them as proof.
entries.myth: The myth is that putting on a guard's uniform turns ordinary people into sadists. In reality, the guards were nudged towards toughness, many stayed decent, and the study was never a controlled experiment.

quiz.q: Why do psychologists no longer treat the Stanford Prison Experiment as strong evidence?
options: The guards refused to wear uniforms
It was run with too many participants
The guards were coached and there was no comparison group
The prisoners knew the guards personally
quiz.why: Coaching by the researchers and the lack of any control condition mean the guards' behaviour cannot be put down to the role itself.

entries.title: The bystander effect
entries.line: Each person is less likely to help in an emergency when they believe other people are also there to respond.
entries.idea: When something goes wrong in front of a crowd, each person may wait for someone else to act. Bibb Latané and John Darley proposed two reasons. The first is diffusion of responsibility: with more people around, each feels less personally on the hook. The second is reading the room: if nobody else looks alarmed, perhaps it is not an emergency after all. Helping also requires noticing the problem, judging it serious, and knowing what to do. Every one of those steps can stall in a group. The key subtlety is this: each individual becomes less likely to help, but in a large crowd the chance that at least one person steps in can still be high.

study.name: The seizure study
study.ref: Darley, J. M., & Latané, B. (1968). Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 8(4), 377-383.
study.story: The study was inspired by the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in New York. Newspapers reported that 38 neighbours watched and did nothing. That account later turned out to be badly exaggerated, but it set Darley and Latané thinking. They invited students to discuss the pressures of college life over an intercom, each in a separate booth, supposedly to protect privacy. Each student believed they were talking with either one, two or five other people. In truth, the other voices were recordings. Early on, one voice mentioned that he sometimes had seizures. Later in the talk, that voice began to stammer, gasp, and say he was having a fit and needed help. Then it choked and went quiet. Only one microphone was on at a time, so the student could not hear what anyone else was doing. The question was simple: would the student leave the booth to find the experimenter, and how quickly? Students who thought they were the only listener mostly rushed out. Students who thought four others could hear often stayed put, looking anxious and unsure. Many who did not help were clearly upset, and several asked afterwards whether the man was all right. They were not cold. They seemed frozen by the thought that someone else was surely dealing with it.
study.finding: When students thought they were the only listener, about 85% went for help before the seizure ended. When they thought four others were listening, only about a third did.

entries.statusNote: The lab effect is real but narrower than the legend. A 2011 meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) by Peter Fischer and colleagues found the effect overall but weaker in clearly dangerous emergencies. A 2020 study by Richard Philpot and colleagues examined CCTV footage of real public conflicts in three countries. In about nine out of ten incidents, at least one bystander intervened. Bigger crowds made it more likely that someone did. The Kitty Genovese story itself was largely wrong. What survives: each person feels less responsible in a crowd, but crowds often still help.
life: If you need help in public, point to one person and give them a specific task, such as 'You in the blue coat, call an ambulance'.
When you see trouble, assume nobody has acted yet. Asking 'Are you okay?' takes seconds and breaks the freeze.
In group chats and shared inboxes, name who is responsible for each task, or everyone will assume someone else has it.
entries.myth: The myth is that crowds make people callous and that Kitty Genovese died while 38 people watched. In fact the Genovese story was exaggerated, and real footage shows that someone usually helps.

quiz.q: Which statement best fits the evidence on bystanders?
options: Larger crowds always mean nobody helps
Each person is less likely to help, yet someone in a crowd often does
Only selfish people fail to help
The effect disappears when people are upset
quiz.why: Responsibility spreads thinly across a group, but with many people present the odds that at least one acts can remain high.

entries.title: Social proof
entries.line: When unsure what to do, people tend to copy what they believe most others like them are doing.
entries.idea: Social proof is using other people's behaviour as a guide to what is right or sensible. Robert Cialdini made the term popular. It is a useful shortcut: if a restaurant is packed, the food is probably decent. It works best when we are uncertain and when the others seem similar to us. Researchers separate two kinds of norm. A descriptive norm is what people actually do. An injunctive norm is what people approve of. Messages that say 'most people do this' can nudge behaviour. They can also backfire. Saying 'too many people litter' quietly tells listeners that littering is normal. That is why careful messages stress the good behaviour of the majority.

study.name: The hotel towel study
study.who: Noah Goldstein, Robert Cialdini, Vladas Griskevicius
study.ref: Goldstein, N. J., Cialdini, R. B., & Griskevicius, V. (2008). A room with a viewpoint: Using social norms to motivate environmental conservation in hotels. Journal of Consumer Research, 35(3), 472-482.
study.story: Many hotels leave a card in the bathroom asking guests to reuse their towels to help the environment. The researchers worked with a mid-sized American hotel to test whether different wording made a difference. Housekeepers placed one of several cards in each room and quietly recorded whether guests hung their towels up to reuse them. One card used the usual green message about protecting nature. Another said that most guests at the hotel had reused their towels at least once during their stay. In a second experiment the team went further. Some cards said that most guests who had stayed in that very room had reused their towels. Others mentioned men and women, or citizens in general. Nothing else about the rooms changed. Guests did not know they were in a study. The towels simply piled up on the floor or hung neatly on the rail. The researchers then compared rates across the different cards. The idea was that a guest alone in a strange room, unsure of the local custom, might look for a clue about what people like them do. The more specific and closer to their own situation the clue felt, the stronger the expected pull.
study.finding: The card saying most guests reused towels raised reuse from about 35% to about 44%. Mentioning previous guests in the same room did a little better again.

entries.statusNote: The core idea is solid, but its famous uses are mixed. That people copy others is one of the best supported ideas in social psychology. Norm messages in the real world, though, usually have small effects. A German repeat of the towel study in 2014 found no benefit from the norm card. Large energy programmes compare households with their neighbours. They have cut use by around 2% on average, which is useful at scale but modest. Effects depend on the audience trusting the claim and feeling similar to the group. What survives: social proof is real and often useful, but norm nudges are not magic.
life: Fake reviews, '1,200 people are viewing this' banners and canned laughter all borrow social proof. Ask whether the crowd is real.
To change a habit in a group, highlight how many people already do the good thing, not how many fail.
When you are unsure, the crowd is a fair starting guess, but check whether those people know more than you.
entries.myth: The myth is that telling people 'everyone does it' reliably changes behaviour. Real-world effects are usually small, and stressing how common a bad habit is can make it worse.

quiz.q: A council wants less litter. Which message best uses social proof?
options: 'Litter is a huge problem here: thousands drop rubbish daily'
'Nine in ten residents here take their rubbish home'
'Littering is illegal'
'Please think of the environment'
quiz.why: Stressing what most people already do sets a positive norm, while describing widespread littering makes it seem normal.

entries.title: Reciprocity
entries.aka: The norm of reciprocity, the rule of return
entries.line: People feel a strong pull to repay favours, even small ones they did not ask for.
entries.idea: Reciprocity is the social rule that we should return what others give us. The sociologist Alvin Gouldner argued in 1960 that it exists in nearly every culture. It helps strangers cooperate, because giving first is less risky when you can expect something back. The rule is powerful enough to be exploited. A small free gift can create a feeling of debt that is out of proportion to the gift. That feeling can override whether we even like the giver. Charities send free address labels, shops hand out samples, and sales staff offer small favours. The urge to repay is usually healthy. The trick is noticing when someone has set it off on purpose.

study.name: The Coke and raffle ticket study
study.ref: Regan, D. T. (1971). Effects of a favor and liking on compliance. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 7(6), 627-639.
study.story: Students at Cornell University signed up for what they were told was a study of art appreciation. Each worked alongside another student, who was in fact a helper of the researcher. Between rating paintings, there was a short break. In some sessions, the helper left the room and came back with two bottles of Coca-Cola. He casually handed one to the volunteer, saying he had bought one for himself and got one for them too. In other sessions he came back empty-handed. In a third version, the researcher himself brought the drinks. At the end of the study, the helper asked a favour. He was selling raffle tickets for a new car, and he would win a prize if he sold the most. Would the volunteer buy some? The tickets cost a quarter each. There was another twist. In some sessions, the helper was pleasant. In others, he acted rudely, to see whether liking him mattered. Afterwards, volunteers rated how much they liked him. The researcher counted the tickets bought in each condition. The question was whether a small, unrequested drink would change how much money people handed over, and whether liking would matter more than the favour itself.
study.finding: Volunteers who had been given a drink bought roughly twice as many tickets as those who had not. Whether they liked the helper mattered much less than the favour.

entries.statusNote: Reciprocity is one of the sturdiest findings in social science. Studies in economics, such as trust games, show that people repay generosity across many cultures. Field studies point the same way. In restaurant studies, small gifts such as mints with the bill have been linked to larger tips. Some of those studies were small, though. Regan's own study has not been copied often in exact form, and the exact sizes of gift effects vary. What survives clearly: unrequested gifts create a felt obligation, and that obligation shapes what people do next.
life: When a seller gives you a free sample or gift, remind yourself you can accept it without owing them a purchase.
Give help or credit to colleagues freely. Goodwill tends to come back, and it builds trust over time.
If a favour feels oddly large for a stranger to offer, ask what they might want in return.
entries.myth: The myth is that we only repay people we like. Regan's study suggests a small favour can drive repayment even towards someone we find unpleasant.

quiz.q: Why do charities often include a small free gift with a donation request?
options: To trigger a feeling that the gift should be repaid
Because gifts are cheaper than stamps
To make the letter heavier and look important
To prove the charity is well funded
quiz.why: An unrequested gift activates the reciprocity norm, making people feel they ought to give something back.

entries.title: Foot in the door
entries.line: Agreeing to a small request can make people more willing to agree to a larger one later.
entries.idea: The foot in the door technique starts small. First you ask for something easy that almost anyone will grant. Later you ask for something bigger. The idea is that saying yes to the first request changes how people see themselves. 'I am the sort of person who supports this cause.' Turning down the second request would then clash with that new self-image. Another explanation is simple commitment: once people have started down a path, they like to stay consistent. The technique seems to work best when the first request takes real, if small, effort, and when both requests serve a cause people care about. It works less well when the first request is trivial or the second one is far too big.

study.name: The 'Drive Carefully' sign study
study.ref: Freedman, J. L., & Fraser, S. C. (1966). Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 4(2), 195-202.
study.story: In a Californian suburb, a researcher posing as a volunteer for a safe driving campaign knocked on doors. To some homeowners, he made a small request. Would they place a little sign, a few inches across, saying 'Be a safe driver' in a window of their home or car? Most said yes. Other homeowners were asked to sign a petition about safe driving or about keeping California beautiful. Two weeks later, a different person visited the same houses, plus a fresh set of houses whose owners had not been contacted before. This time the request was outrageous. He showed a photograph of a lovely house almost hidden behind a huge, badly lettered sign reading 'Drive Carefully'. Would they let volunteers dig holes and put a sign like that on their front lawn for a week or so? Most of the fresh homeowners refused politely. It was ugly and would ruin the look of their homes. But among those who had already agreed to the little sticker, many said yes. Even people whose first request was about a different topic, such as keeping California beautiful, were more willing than the newcomers. That suggested the first yes had changed something about how they saw themselves, not just their view of road safety.
study.finding: About 76% of homeowners who had agreed to the small safe driving sign accepted the giant lawn sign. Only about 17% of those approached for the first time did.

entries.statusNote: The effect is real but much smaller and less reliable than the famous study suggests. Meta-analyses pool the results of many studies. Several in the 1980s, and a review by Jerry Burger in 1999, found that the average boost is small. Many studies show no effect at all. It works best for prosocial causes and when the first request needs some effort. It also helps when people are reminded of their earlier help. It can fail or backfire if the first request is refused or the jump is too large. What survives: small commitments can nudge later choices, modestly.
life: To build a habit, start with a tiny step, such as one press-up a day. A small yes to yourself makes a bigger one easier.
If a salesperson asks a string of easy questions you agree with, notice the trap of consistency before the big ask.
Volunteer organisers can invite people to a short, easy task first before asking for regular commitments.
entries.myth: The myth is that getting one small yes all but guarantees a big one. In most studies, the effect is small, and it often fails when the requests are unrelated or the leap is large.

quiz.q: According to one leading explanation, why does foot in the door work?
options: The first request makes people tired
Agreeing once changes how people see themselves, so refusing later feels inconsistent
People feel they owe a concession after refusing
The second requester seems more trustworthy
quiz.why: The self-perception account says the first yes shapes self-image, and a later refusal would clash with it.

entries.title: Door in the face
entries.line: After people refuse a large request, they become more willing to grant a smaller one from the same person.
entries.idea: Door in the face is the reverse of foot in the door. You start with a request so large it is almost sure to be refused. Then you retreat to the smaller request you wanted all along. People often agree to the second, more than if you had asked for it straight away. The leading explanation is reciprocity: the asker has made a concession, so the other person feels they should make one too. Guilt about refusing and contrast also play a part, since the second request seems modest next to the first. The technique works best when the same person makes both requests, with no long gap between them, and for good causes.

study.name: The zoo trip study
study.ref: Cialdini, R. B., Vincent, J. E., Lewis, S. K., Catalan, J., Wheeler, D., & Darby, B. L. (1975). Reciprocal concessions procedure for inducing compliance: The door-in-the-face technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 31(2), 206-215.
study.story: On a university campus in Arizona, researchers posing as members of a county youth programme stopped students walking alone. To some, they made an enormous request. Would the student volunteer as an unpaid counsellor for young offenders, for two hours a week, for at least two years? Not one student agreed. The researcher then said something like 'Oh, well, we also have another programme you might help with'. Would the student chaperone a group of young offenders on a two-hour trip to the zoo? A second group of students heard only the zoo request, with no big ask first. A third group heard both requests described together and were asked to choose one, which let the researchers test whether simple contrast explained the result. The zoo trip was not an appealing prospect. It meant giving up an afternoon to supervise troubled teenagers with strangers. Yet the researchers found a striking difference. Students who had just turned down the two-year commitment were far more willing to say yes to the zoo trip. In the conditions where no concession took place, agreement stayed low. The team argued this showed it was the act of retreating, of seeming to give ground, that made people want to meet the asker halfway.
study.finding: About half of the students who first refused the large request agreed to the zoo trip. Only about one in six of those asked about the zoo alone agreed.

entries.statusNote: Real but modest. Meta-analyses, which pool many studies, find a reliable but small effect overall. It is stronger when the same person makes both requests, when the second follows straight away, and when the cause is prosocial. A 2012 meta-analysis by Thomas Feeley and colleagues found it raised spoken agreement more reliably than actual follow-through. In 2021, Oliver Genschow and colleagues ran a large preregistered replication of the zoo study. Preregistered means the plan was fixed in advance, so results could not be cherry-picked. The technique still worked. What survives: retreating from a big ask does raise agreement to a smaller one, but modestly.
life: If a seller shows you the most expensive option first, then a 'sensible' one, notice whether the second only looks reasonable by comparison.
When you refuse a large request, judge the smaller follow-up on its own merits. Ask whether you would have said yes to it first.
When fundraising, a modest ask after a bigger one can work, but use it honestly and sparingly.
entries.myth: The myth is that any outrageous first offer will make any second offer acceptable. The effect is small, and it mostly works when the same person asks twice in quick succession.

quiz.q: Which situation fits the door in the face technique?
options: Asking for a small favour, then a big one
Asking a friend for £500, then for £50 after they refuse
Offering a free gift, then asking for a donation
Saying stock is running out
quiz.why: The technique begins with a large request that is refused, then retreats to the smaller request that was the real goal.

entries.title: Cognitive dissonance
entries.aka: Dissonance theory, effort justification, induced compliance
entries.line: When our actions clash with our beliefs, we feel uncomfortable and often change the belief to fit what we did.
entries.idea: Leon Festinger proposed that holding two ideas that clash feels unpleasant. He called that tension cognitive dissonance. People are driven to reduce it. Changing your behaviour is hard after the fact, so people often adjust their beliefs instead. A smoker might decide the health risks are exaggerated. Someone who endured a harsh initiation might decide the group is wonderful. The theory makes a surprising prediction: the less outside reason you have for doing something, the more you need to justify it to yourself. A large reward or a threat gives an easy excuse. A small one does not, so the mind does more work to make the act seem right.

study.name: The one dollar study
study.ref: Festinger, L., & Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203-210.
study.story: Male students at Stanford arrived for what they thought was a study of performance. For an hour they did deliberately mind-numbing tasks. First they put spools on a tray, emptied it, and filled it again. Then they turned square pegs on a board a quarter turn at a time, over and over. When the hour was up, the experimenter explained, with some embarrassment, that his assistant had not turned up. Could the student help? The next participant was waiting outside, and the job was simply to tell her the tasks had been enjoyable and interesting. Some students were offered one dollar for this small lie. Others were offered twenty dollars, a lot of money at the time. A third group did the tasks but were not asked to lie at all. Most students agreed, went out, and told the waiting young woman, who was in on the study, that the tasks had been fun. Then each student was sent to another office to answer what looked like a routine department survey. One question asked how enjoyable the tasks had really been. The researchers expected that the students paid twenty dollars had an easy excuse for their lie. The students paid just one dollar did not, and might have to persuade themselves.
study.finding: Students paid one dollar rated the dull tasks as more enjoyable than those paid twenty dollars or those not asked to lie.

entries.statusNote: Dissonance theory has produced hundreds of studies, and the general idea that people justify their choices is widely accepted. But some classic methods have problems. In 2010, Keith Chen and Jane Risen studied a popular 'free choice' method. They showed it could produce dissonance-like results through a statistical artefact alone. In 2024, David Vaidis led a large replication, a repeat of the study run in many labs at once. It tested the essay version of induced compliance with thousands of people, and it did not find the predicted attitude change. What survives: self-justification is real in everyday life, but some lab effects are weaker or less certain than once believed.
life: After a big purchase, notice if you start hunting only for reviews that praise it. That is dissonance reduction at work.
If you want to keep a promise, say it publicly. People work hard to keep actions and statements in line.
When you catch yourself rationalising a mistake, try simply admitting it. It ends the need for ever more elaborate excuses.
entries.myth: The myth is that big rewards always change minds most. Dissonance theory predicts the reverse in some cases, though modern replications suggest the classic lab effects are less dependable than textbooks imply.

quiz.q: In Festinger and Carlsmith's study, why did the one dollar group rate the tasks as more enjoyable?
options: They were paid more per minute
They had no strong outside reason for lying, so they adjusted their belief
They were less bored than the others
They had been told the tasks were fun beforehand
quiz.why: A small reward gave too little justification for the lie, so students reduced the tension by deciding the tasks were not so bad.

entries.title: Scarcity
entries.line: Things seem more valuable when they are rare, running out, or available only for a limited time.
entries.idea: Scarcity is the tendency to want something more when it is hard to get. One reason is a sensible shortcut: rare things are often rare because they are good or popular. Another is reactance, a term for the urge to push back when our freedom to choose is threatened. If an option might vanish, we want to keep it open. Scarcity is most powerful when it is new and when it seems to be caused by other people wanting the same thing. Advertisers use it constantly: 'only three left', 'offer ends tonight', 'limited edition'. The effect is real, but it can also make us rush into decisions and pay for urgency rather than quality.

study.name: The cookie jar study
study.who: Stephen Worchel, Jerry Lee, Akanbi Adewole
study.ref: Worchel, S., Lee, J., & Adewole, A. (1975). Effects of supply and demand on ratings of object value. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(5), 906-914.
study.story: Students taking part in what they believed was a consumer study sat down in front of a glass jar of chocolate chip cookies. They were asked to take one, taste it, and rate how much they liked it, how attractive it was, and how much it should cost. For some students, the jar held ten cookies. For others, it held only two. That was the first test: would the very same cookie seem better when there were fewer of them? The researchers then added a twist. Some students started with a jar of ten. Just before tasting, the experimenter swapped it for a jar holding only two. Sometimes the reason given was that other participants had eaten more than expected, so supply had run low because of demand. Other times, the reason was an accident: the experimenter had simply given out the wrong jar. A further group saw their jar go from two cookies to ten. The cookies were identical in every condition. Only the number in the jar, and the story behind it, changed. The students carefully nibbled their single cookie, filled in their ratings, and left, unaware that the jar, not the biscuit, was the real subject of the study.
study.finding: Cookies from the nearly empty jar were rated more desirable. They were rated highest when the supply had just dropped because other people wanted them.

entries.statusNote: Reviews of scarcity research found that scarcity does tend to raise how much people value things. One was a 1991 meta-analysis, which pools many studies, by Michael Lynn. Marketing studies often find similar effects. But effects vary a lot by product and setting. Scarcity can make an item seem low quality, or it can simply irritate shoppers who see through it. The cookie study itself has rarely been repeated exactly. What survives: scarcity cues reliably grab attention and usually raise perceived value, but the size of the effect depends heavily on context.
life: When a site says 'only two left' or shows a countdown, pause. Ask whether you would want it at the same price with no timer.
Before a sale, set your budget and list of needs in advance, so urgency messages cannot rewrite them.
If a shortage is caused by other people's demand, remember that their rush does not tell you whether it suits you.
entries.myth: The myth is that scarcity always increases desire. Sometimes it backfires, making a product look unpopular or a seller look pushy, and the effect varies a lot.

quiz.q: In the cookie study, when were the cookies rated most desirable?
options: When the jar went from two to ten cookies
When the jar held ten cookies throughout
When the jar dropped from ten to two because others had eaten them
When the jar dropped from ten to two by accident
quiz.why: New scarcity caused by other people's demand produced the highest ratings, combining rarity with a sign of popularity.

entries.title: The fundamental attribution error
entries.line: We tend to explain other people's behaviour by their personality, while underestimating the power of their situation.
entries.idea: When someone cuts us up in traffic, we think 'what an idiot', not 'maybe they are rushing to hospital'. That is the fundamental attribution error. Lee Ross named it in 1977. We see the person clearly, but the pressures acting on them are often invisible. So we credit their character for behaviour that the situation largely caused. It is also called correspondence bias, meaning we assume actions correspond to inner traits. The bias seems stronger when we are busy or tired, because correcting for the situation takes extra effort. It may also be weaker in cultures that pay more attention to context and relationships.

study.name: The Castro essay study
study.ref: Jones, E. E., & Harris, V. A. (1967). The attribution of attitudes. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 3(1), 1-24.
study.story: In the 1960s, Fidel Castro was a deeply divisive figure in the United States. Edward Jones and Victor Harris used that to design a clever test. American college students read a short essay supposedly written by another student. Some essays praised Castro's Cuba. Others attacked it. Then the readers estimated what the writer truly thought about Castro. The key twist was in what the readers were told about how the essay came to be written. Some heard that the writer had freely chosen which side to argue. Others heard that a debate coach or a course instructor had assigned the side, so the writer had no choice at all. When the writer had chosen freely, it made sense to assume the essay showed their real opinion. But when the side had been assigned, the essay should have told readers very little. After all, it was a set exercise, like a debating club motion. The researchers wanted to know whether readers would make that adjustment. They also varied how persuasive and enthusiastic the essays sounded. The readers knew all the facts. They had been told clearly about the assignment. The only question was whether they would use that knowledge when judging the person behind the words.
study.finding: Even when readers knew the writer had been assigned a side, they judged pro-Castro writers to be more pro-Castro. Free choice made the gap larger, but did not create it.

entries.statusNote: The basic lab result, that people under-adjust for situational pressure, has been repeated many times. But the broader claim needs care. Cross-cultural work suggests East Asian participants more often consider the situation. Examples include studies by Michael Morris and Kaiping Peng in the 1990s. A related claim is that we explain others by traits but ourselves by situations. A 2006 meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) by Bertram Malle found that effect close to zero on average. What survives: people often over-read character from behaviour, but the error is not universal or always 'fundamental'.
life: When a colleague misses a deadline, ask about their workload before deciding they are lazy.
Before judging someone in a viral video, imagine three situations that could explain what they did.
Be aware that others may misjudge you in the same way. Give context when you behave out of character.
entries.myth: The myth is that this bias is fixed and universal. It varies by culture and setting, and the idea that we always excuse ourselves but blame others has weak support.

quiz.q: A waiter is curt with you on a very busy night. What would the fundamental attribution error lead you to conclude?
options: The restaurant is understaffed
The waiter is a rude person
You probably caught them at a bad moment
The kitchen is behind with orders
quiz.why: The error is explaining behaviour by personality while neglecting the situation, such as how busy the restaurant is.

entries.title: In-group bias and minimal groups
entries.aka: In-group favouritism, the minimal group paradigm
entries.line: Even when grouped on trivial or random grounds, people favour members of their own group over outsiders.
entries.idea: In-group bias is the habit of treating 'us' better than 'them'. Henri Tajfel wanted to find the smallest possible basis for it. He discovered that very little is needed. Put people into groups using a meaningless label, with no history, no contact, and no conflict, and they still favour their own side. This became known as the minimal group paradigm. Tajfel and John Turner later explained it with social identity theory. People get part of their sense of self from the groups they belong to, so they want those groups to look good. A key detail is that the bias is mostly about favouring the in-group. Active hostility to the out-group is a separate step and is less automatic.

study.name: The Klee and Kandinsky study
study.who: Henri Tajfel, Michael Billig, Robert Bundy, Claude Flament
study.ref: Tajfel, H., Billig, M. G., Bundy, R. P., & Flament, C. (1971). Social categorization and intergroup behaviour. European Journal of Social Psychology, 1(2), 149-178.
study.story: Teenage schoolboys in Bristol came into a university lab in small groups. Most of them knew each other from school. They were shown slides of abstract paintings and asked which ones they preferred. Afterwards, each boy was told privately that he belonged to the group that liked Paul Klee, or the group that liked Wassily Kandinsky. In fact, the groups were assigned at random. Then each boy went into a cubicle on his own. He had a booklet of tables, and his task was to share out small amounts of real money between two other boys. He knew only their code numbers and whether each one was a Klee fan or a Kandinsky fan. He never met them and could not give money to himself. Some tables let him give the most to both boys. Others let him favour his own group, but only if both boys ended up with less in total. There was nothing to gain personally, no history between the groups, and no rivalry. The labels were based on a few minutes of looking at art. And yet, booklet after booklet, the boys tilted the money towards their own side. Many chose options that widened the gap between groups even when that meant their own group got less than it could have.
study.finding: Boys consistently gave more to members of their own meaningless group. They often preferred to maximise the difference between groups rather than the total gain for their own side.

entries.statusNote: Minimal group effects have been repeated in many countries and age groups, including young children. Meta-analyses (studies pooling many studies) on in-group bias, such as one by Brian Mullen and colleagues in 1992, confirm it is robust. A 2014 meta-analysis by Daniel Balliet and colleagues found that people cooperate more with in-group members across many cultures. Researchers note that the bias in minimal groups is mostly favouritism rather than hostility. Effects can be smaller when people are asked to dish out harms instead of rewards. What survives: very small cues of belonging are enough to tilt how we treat others.
life: Notice how quickly teams at work or fans of a sports club start to see the other side as worse. The label alone can do that.
When hiring or judging, check whether shared schools, hobbies or home towns are quietly earning someone extra credit.
To bring rival groups together, create a shared identity or goal that includes both of them.
entries.myth: The myth is that groups must clash over something real before bias appears. Tajfel showed that random labels are enough, though the bias is more about favouring 'us' than hating 'them'.

quiz.q: What was most surprising about the minimal group results?
options: Boys favoured friends from school
Bias appeared even though groups were random and nothing was at stake
Boys gave themselves the most money
Kandinsky fans were more generous than Klee fans
quiz.why: The groups were meaningless and the boys gained nothing personally, yet they still favoured their own side.

entries.title: The halo effect
entries.aka: Halo error, 'what is beautiful is good'
entries.line: One good trait, such as looks or warmth, colours how we judge a person's other, unrelated qualities.
entries.idea: The halo effect is when one impression spreads to everything else we think about a person or thing. Edward Thorndike named it in 1920, after noticing that army officers who rated a soldier highly on one quality rated him highly on nearly all of them. Attractive, warm or confident people tend to be seen as smarter, kinder and more capable, even with no evidence. It works in reverse too, sometimes called the horns effect: one bad trait drags down the rest. Halo effects also shape how we judge products, brands and companies. The tricky part is that we usually do not notice it. We feel we are judging each quality separately when we are not.

study.name: The warm and cold lecturer study
study.ref: Nisbett, R. E., & Wilson, T. D. (1977). The halo effect: Evidence for unconscious alteration of judgments. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 35(4), 250-256.
study.story: University students watched a video interview with a college lecturer who spoke English with a strong Belgian accent. There were two versions, filmed with the same man. In one, he was warm and friendly. He spoke enthusiastically about teaching, said he liked his students, and was flexible about how he ran his classes. In the other, he was cold and distant. He seemed rigid, distrustful of students, and impatient. Each student saw only one version. Afterwards, they rated how much they liked him. They also rated three things that did not change between the videos: his physical appearance, his mannerisms, and his accent. Every one of those was exactly the same in both films. Finally, the researchers asked students a revealing question. Had their liking for the lecturer affected their ratings of his looks, mannerisms and accent? Or was it the other way round? The students who had seen the cold version had something to explain. They found his appearance, mannerisms and accent less appealing. When asked why, many insisted that his irritating accent and mannerisms were the reason they disliked him. They did not realise that his warmth, or lack of it, was shaping how everything else about him looked and sounded.
study.finding: Students who saw the warm version rated the lecturer's appearance, mannerisms and accent as more appealing. They denied that liking him had influenced those judgements.

entries.statusNote: Halo effects appear across many settings, from job appraisals to teacher marking to consumer ratings. Meta-analyses (studies pooling many studies) of physical attractiveness, such as one by Alice Eagly and colleagues in 1991, found that attractive people are judged more favourably. The effect was strongest on social qualities such as likeability, and weaker on traits such as integrity. Some halo in ratings may reflect real links between traits rather than pure error, which makes it hard to measure exactly. The specific Nisbett and Wilson study had a modest sample and has rarely been copied directly. What survives: one striking trait reliably spills over into unrelated judgements.
life: In interviews, score each skill separately against set criteria before forming an overall view. It limits one strong first impression.
Notice when a celebrity endorsement makes you trust a product they know nothing about.
When marking or reviewing work, hide names and photos where you can, so reputation does not tint the score.
entries.myth: The myth is that attractive people are judged better on everything. The effect is strongest for social traits and much weaker for qualities such as honesty or concern for others.

quiz.q: What did Nisbett and Wilson's students get wrong about their own judgements?
options: They thought the lecturer was Belgian
They believed his accent caused their dislike, when his coldness shaped their view of his accent
They rated the warm lecturer as cold
They refused to rate his appearance
quiz.why: The students reversed the cause: his warmth or coldness tinted their ratings, but they blamed his accent and mannerisms.

entries.title: The contact hypothesis
entries.line: Positive contact between members of different groups tends to reduce prejudice, especially under equal and cooperative conditions.
entries.idea: The contact hypothesis says that getting to know people from another group can reduce prejudice against them. Gordon Allport set it out in his 1954 book, The Nature of Prejudice. He argued it works best under four conditions. The groups should have equal status in the setting. They should share common goals. They should work together rather than compete. And the contact should have support from authorities or local norms. Contact may help by reducing anxiety, building empathy, and giving people real information in place of stereotypes. Friendship across groups appears especially powerful. Later research suggests that even knowing that a friend has an out-group friend can help.

study.name: Football teams in post-ISIS Iraq
study.ref: Mousa, S. (2020). Building social cohesion between Christians and Muslims through soccer in post-ISIS Iraq. Science, 369(6505), 866-870.
study.story: After the so-called Islamic State was pushed out of northern Iraq, many Christians returned to towns where trust in their Muslim neighbours had been badly damaged. The political scientist Salma Mousa set up an amateur football league for Christian men who had been displaced. Teams were mostly Christian, but she added a twist. By random assignment, some teams received several Muslim players, while others were all Christian. Random assignment was important, because people who choose mixed teams might already be more open-minded. The league played for a couple of months, with regular training and matches. Mousa then measured what changed. Some measures were about behaviour on the pitch and around it. Did Christian players vote for a Muslim from another team as the league's best sportsman? Did they sign up to train with Muslims again after the season ended? Other measures looked beyond the league. Would the Christian players visit a café or restaurant in a nearby Muslim town? Would they attend a mixed social event? Mousa also asked about general attitudes towards Muslims. The design allowed her to separate contact in a cooperative setting from contact outside it, and both from shifts in stated beliefs.
study.finding: Christian players with Muslim teammates were more likely to vote for a Muslim player for a sportsmanship award. They were also more likely to train with Muslims later. Effects on wider attitudes, and on behaviour outside the league, were weak.

entries.statusNote: In 2006, Thomas Pettigrew and Linda Tropp ran a major meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies). It combined over 500 studies and found that contact is linked to less prejudice. This held even when Allport's conditions were not all met. But most of those studies only showed a correlation, a link rather than proof of cause. In 2019, Elizabeth Levy Paluck and colleagues reviewed randomised experiments, where contact is assigned by chance. On average the effects were positive. But they were smaller for race and ethnicity, and rarely tracked over long periods. What survives: contact generally helps, especially in cooperative settings, but effects may be modest and local.
life: If you want to bridge a divide at work or in your community, set up shared projects with a common goal, not just social mixers.
Make friends across groups when you can. Close, repeated contact does more than a single polite meeting.
When contact goes badly or is forced and competitive, it can harden attitudes. Design the setting with care.
entries.myth: The myth is that simply putting groups side by side ends prejudice. Contact helps most when it is cooperative and equal, and changes often stay within the setting where they happened.

quiz.q: What did Mousa's Iraqi football study show about contact?
options: It had no effect on anything
It changed behaviour towards Muslim teammates, but wider effects were weak
It reversed all prejudice in the towns
It made attitudes worse
quiz.why: Behaviour linked to the league improved, but the change did not clearly spread to wider attitudes or other settings.

entries.title: Self-determination theory
entries.line: People thrive and stay motivated when they feel autonomy, competence and connection to others.
entries.idea: Self-determination theory says motivation comes in different kinds, not just different amounts. Doing something because you enjoy it or value it is 'autonomous' motivation. Doing it to win a reward, dodge a punishment or avoid guilt is 'controlled' motivation. The theory, built by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, claims we all share three basic needs. We need autonomy (feeling that our actions are our own), competence (feeling capable) and relatedness (feeling connected to others). When our surroundings meet these needs, we persist longer, learn more deeply and feel better. When they are thwarted, by pressure, constant surveillance or coldness, motivation turns brittle. The theory has been applied at work, in schools, in sport and in health care.

study.name: The Soma puzzle study
study.ref: Deci, E. L. (1971). Effects of externally mediated rewards on intrinsic motivation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 18(1), 105-115.
study.story: Edward Deci, a young psychologist, wanted to know what money does to enjoyment. He invited students to his lab for three sessions. Each time they worked on Soma puzzles, a set of oddly shaped blocks that can be fitted together into many different figures. Most people find them absorbing. In the middle session, half the students were paid a dollar for each puzzle they solved. The other half did the same puzzles for nothing. Then came the clever part. Partway through each session, Deci made an excuse to leave the room for a few minutes. The student was left alone with more puzzles, some magazines and nothing in particular to do. Out of sight, the experimenter timed how long each person kept playing with the puzzles, although nobody had asked them to. This 'free-choice' time became a measure of genuine interest. In the final session, nobody was paid. The students who had been paid now spent less of their free time on the puzzles than they had at the start. The unpaid students showed no such drop. Deci argued that the payment had shifted their reason for playing, from 'I like this' to 'I do this for money'. Over the following decades, that idea grew into self-determination theory.
study.finding: Once payment stopped, students who had been paid spent less free time on the puzzles. Unpaid students kept their interest.

entries.statusNote: The broad theory has strong support. Hundreds of studies across many countries link the three needs to wellbeing, persistence and performance. Meta-analyses (studies that pool the results of many studies) of programmes that train teachers, coaches and doctors to support autonomy find real benefits, mostly small to moderate. Critics note that much of the evidence is correlational, meaning it shows links rather than proving cause, and relies on questionnaires. The theory is also broad enough to be hard to prove wrong. Its specific claim that rewards undermine interest is narrower and more disputed (see the overjustification effect).
life: To motivate someone, offer real choices and explain the reasons behind rules, rather than relying on pressure or prizes.
If your own drive is fading, ask which need is starved: freedom, a sense of progress, or people around you.
Be wary of workplaces that track every keystroke: heavy surveillance can turn willing effort into grudging compliance.
entries.myth: Myth: motivation is a single tank that is either full or empty. In fact the kind of motivation matters, and freely chosen reasons tend to last longer than pressure.

quiz.q: According to self-determination theory, which manager is most likely to sustain her team's motivation?
options: One who offers a big bonus for hitting targets
One who explains why the work matters and lets people choose how to do it
One who checks progress every hour to keep everyone focused
One who warns that poor performers will be named in meetings
quiz.why: Explaining reasons and offering choice support autonomy, which the theory says sustains motivation better than bonuses, surveillance or threats.

entries.title: The overjustification effect
entries.aka: The hidden cost of reward; crowding out
entries.line: Expected rewards for something people already enjoy can reduce their interest once the rewards stop.
entries.idea: The overjustification effect is what can happen when you reward people for something they already like. A child loves drawing. You start giving her a prize for every picture. Later the prizes stop, and she draws less than she did before. One explanation is that people watch their own behaviour to work out why they do things. With a reward on offer, 'I draw because I enjoy it' becomes 'I draw to get prizes'. Self-determination theory adds that rewards can feel controlling. The effect is strongest when rewards are tangible, expected and given simply for doing the task. Surprise rewards, praise and rewards for doing a task well are much less harmful, and are sometimes helpful.

study.name: The Good Player Award
study.who: Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett
study.ref: Lepper, M. R., Greene, D., & Nisbett, R. E. (1973). Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward: A test of the 'overjustification' hypothesis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 28(1), 129-137.
study.story: Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett ran their study at a nursery school on the Stanford University campus. First they watched the children during free play to find those who already liked drawing with felt-tip markers. These were children who chose the markers on their own, with nobody asking. Each of these children was later taken to a separate room and invited to draw. Some were told beforehand that they could win a 'Good Player Award', a certificate with a gold seal and a ribbon. They drew, and received it. A second group got the same certificate as a surprise at the end. A third group got no award at all. About two weeks later, the markers quietly reappeared in the classroom. Observers recorded how long each child spent drawing, with no rewards on offer. The children who had drawn in order to win the award now spent roughly half as much time with the markers as the other two groups. They also drew less than they had before the study began. The children who got the surprise award showed no such drop. So the reward itself did not dampen interest. What mattered was drawing in order to get it.
study.finding: Children who drew expecting an award later spent about half as much free time drawing. Children given a surprise award, or none, showed no such drop.

entries.statusNote: The effect is real but narrower than often claimed. A 1999 meta-analysis (a study that pools many studies) by Edward Deci, Richard Koestner and Richard Ryan combined 128 experiments. It found that expected, tangible rewards for doing an interesting task reliably lower later interest, while praise tended to raise it. Judy Cameron and David Pierce argued that the harm is small and avoidable, and the dispute ran for years. Most experiments use short lab tasks. For dull tasks, or work people would not do anyway, rewards usually raise effort and do little harm.
life: If a child already loves reading, praise their effort and choices rather than paying them per book.
Use rewards for tasks nobody enjoys, like filing or chores, where there is little interest to undermine.
If a hobby starts to feel like a job after you begin selling your work, keep some of it purely for fun.
entries.myth: Myth: rewards always kill motivation. In fact the harm comes mostly from expected, tangible rewards for things people already enjoy; for boring tasks, rewards usually work.

quiz.q: Which reward is least likely to undermine a child's love of painting?
options: A promised sweet for every painting
A surprise sticker given once, afterwards
Pocket money for each hour spent painting
A prize for whoever paints the most pictures
quiz.why: An unexpected reward cannot become the reason for painting, so it does not shift the child's motive from enjoyment to payment.

entries.title: Goal-setting theory
entries.line: Specific, challenging goals usually lead to better performance than vague goals such as 'do your best'.
entries.idea: Goal-setting theory, developed by Edwin Locke and Gary Latham, is one of the best-tested ideas in work psychology. Its core claim is simple. Clear, difficult goals beat easy goals, and they beat the vague instruction to 'do your best'. Goals work by focusing attention, raising effort, increasing persistence and prompting people to search for better strategies. They work best when people are committed to them, get feedback on their progress and have the skills needed. There are limits. On complex tasks that people are still learning, a goal to discover good strategies works better than a goal for an outcome. And goals that are too narrow or too high can encourage corner-cutting, risk-taking or cheating.

study.name: The logging trucks
study.who: Gary Latham and J. James Baldes
study.ref: Latham, G. P., & Baldes, J. J. (1975). The 'practical significance' of Locke's theory of goal setting. Journal of Applied Psychology, 60(1), 122-124.
study.story: In the early 1970s, a timber company in the north-western United States had a costly problem. Its drivers were hauling logs from the forest to the mill in trucks loaded well below the legal weight limit. Each light load meant more trips, more fuel and more wear on the trucks. Telling the drivers to 'do their best' had not helped. Gary Latham and J. James Baldes tried something else. The drivers were given a specific, demanding goal: load each truck to 94 per cent of its legal maximum. There were no rewards for meeting the goal and no punishments for missing it. Nobody was taught a new way to load. The drivers were simply given a target, and their loads were weighed as usual. Before the goal, trucks had carried around 60 per cent of the limit. Over the following months, loads rose sharply, and drivers regularly carried more than 90 per cent. The improvement lasted. Some drivers reportedly turned it into a game, competing to see who came closest to the target. The company estimated that it saved a large sum, partly because it no longer needed to buy extra trucks. A plain number, written down and measured, had changed behaviour where encouragement had failed.
study.finding: Once given a specific, hard goal, drivers raised their loads sharply. Average loads rose from around 60 per cent of the legal limit to over 90 per cent.

entries.statusNote: Few findings in applied psychology have more support. Hundreds of studies, in labs and in workplaces, show that specific, hard goals raise performance compared with vague ones. A 2002 review by Locke and Latham summarised decades of consistent results. The effects are smaller for complex tasks and for groups. Researchers have also documented real costs. Narrow targets can push people to cheat, take risks or neglect anything that is not measured, a problem one 2009 paper called 'goals gone wild'. So the effect holds, but goals need careful design.
life: Swap 'get fitter' for something specific and stretching, such as 'run 5 km in under 30 minutes by June'.
When learning something new, set a goal to try three strategies rather than to hit a score.
Be wary of workplace targets that reward one number: they can quietly encourage gaming or cutting corners.
entries.myth: Myth: 'just do your best' is the kindest and most effective instruction. In fact people usually do better with a clear, challenging target, as long as it is realistic and they have the skills.

quiz.q: A sales team is learning a brand-new, complicated product. Which goal does the research suggest is best at first?
options: Close 50 deals this month
Do your best
Learn and test three different ways of explaining the product
Beat last year's sales figures
quiz.why: On complex tasks people are still learning, goals about finding good strategies tend to work better than outcome targets.

entries.title: Implementation intentions
entries.line: Deciding exactly when, where and how you will act ('if X, then I will do Y') makes follow-through more likely.
entries.idea: An implementation intention is a plan in 'if-then' form. Instead of 'I will exercise more', you decide: 'If it is 7am on Monday, then I will put on my trainers and walk to the park.' The idea comes from the German psychologist Peter Gollwitzer. Good intentions often fail at the moment of action. We forget, get distracted or miss the chance. An if-then plan links a specific cue to a specific response, so the situation itself prompts the behaviour. Acting then needs less willpower and less deciding on the spot. These plans can also help people resist temptation: 'If I am offered dessert, then I will order mint tea.'

study.name: The Christmas Eve report
study.ref: Gollwitzer, P. M., & Brandstätter, V. (1997). Implementation intentions and effective goal pursuit. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 73(1), 186-199.
study.story: Just before the Christmas break, Peter Gollwitzer and Veronika Brandstätter gave university students in Germany a seasonal task. Over the holidays, they were to write a short report on how they had spent Christmas Eve. The report had to be written within a couple of days of Christmas Eve, a tight window in a busy season full of family meals and visits. Half the students were asked to form an implementation intention. They wrote down exactly when and where, in those two days, they would sit down to write the report. The other half received the same task but made no such plan. Everyone intended to do it, and the question was who actually would. When the reports came back, the difference was striking. More than two-thirds of the planners sent in their report on time. Among those who had made no specific plan, only about one in three did. The plan took a minute to write and needed no extra motivation or reward. It simply decided in advance when the moment had arrived, which made it harder to let that moment slip past. The study became a classic example of how a tiny piece of planning can close the gap between meaning to do something and doing it.
study.finding: More than two-thirds of students who planned when and where to write sent the report on time. Only about a third of those with no plan did.

entries.statusNote: The basic effect has held up well. A 2006 meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) by Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran combined 94 studies and found a medium to large effect on reaching goals. Later reviews confirm benefits for health behaviour, such as attending screening, getting vaccinated and exercising. Real-world effects are often smaller than in early lab studies, and publication bias (positive results being more likely to be published) may inflate the average. Plans also help less when people are not committed to the goal. Still, as a cheap, low-risk tool, it has a strong track record.
life: Turn each vague resolution into an 'if-then' sentence that names a time, a place and a first action.
Plan for obstacles too: 'If I feel too tired after work, then I will do just ten minutes.'
Notice that apps asking 'When will you do this?' are borrowing the same trick to keep you coming back.
entries.myth: Myth: following through is all about willpower. In fact a precise plan lets the situation do much of the work, so you need less willpower in the moment.

quiz.q: Which of these is an implementation intention?
options: I want to read more books this year
If I get on the train home, then I will open my book instead of my phone
Reading is important for my career
I will read 20 books this year
quiz.why: An implementation intention links a specific situation (getting on the train) to a specific action (opening the book).

entries.title: How habits form
entries.line: Habits form when an action is repeated in a stable context, gradually becoming automatic over weeks to months.
entries.idea: A habit is an action that a familiar situation triggers automatically, with little thought. Psychologists describe habits as links between a context and a response. The context can be a place, a time of day, a preceding action or even a mood. Each time you do the same thing in the same setting, the link grows a little stronger. Eventually the cue alone sets the action going, even if your goals have changed. That is why habits are so useful when they are good, and so stubborn when they are bad. Building a habit works best by attaching the new action to an existing routine, such as flossing right after brushing. Breaking one often works best by changing the cues rather than fighting temptation head on.

study.name: The 12-week habit study
study.who: Phillippa Lally, Cornelia van Jaarsveld, Henry Potts and Jane Wardle
study.ref: Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W., & Wardle, J. (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998-1009.
study.story: Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London wanted to know how long it really takes to form a habit. Popular advice claimed 21 days, but nobody had tracked it carefully. They recruited 96 volunteers. Each person chose one healthy behaviour to do once a day in the same situation. Examples included eating a piece of fruit with lunch, drinking a bottle of water after breakfast or going for a run before dinner. Every day for 12 weeks, the volunteers logged on to a website. They reported whether they had done the behaviour and answered questions about how automatic it felt. Did they do it without thinking? Would it feel odd not to? The researchers then plotted a curve for each person. For most, automaticity rose quickly at first and then levelled off, like a hill flattening into a plateau. The typical time to reach that plateau was 66 days. But the range was enormous, from 18 days to an estimated 254. Simple actions, like drinking water, became automatic faster than effortful ones, like doing sit-ups. Missing a single day did not seriously set people back. Not everyone completed the study, and some never reached a plateau. Still, the message was clear: habits take weeks to months, not three weeks.
study.finding: Automaticity rose and then levelled off after a median (middle value) of 66 days. Times varied hugely between people and behaviours, from about 18 to 254 days.

entries.statusNote: The core principle is well supported. Decades of research, including work by Wendy Wood and her colleagues, show that repetition in a stable context builds automaticity. The specific numbers are softer. Lally's study was small, relied on self-reports and lost participants along the way. Several estimates were also projected beyond the 12 weeks actually measured. A 2024 systematic review (a careful survey of all relevant studies) found that habits typically took around two months to form. But the range ran from weeks to many months. So treat '66 days' as a rough average, not a rule.
life: Anchor a new habit to something you already do daily: 'after I pour my morning coffee, I will stretch for two minutes'.
To break a habit, change the cues: move the biscuit tin out of sight, or charge your phone outside the bedroom.
Do not give up after a missed day; one lapse barely dents the process.
entries.myth: Myth: it takes 21 days to form a habit. In Lally's study the typical figure was about 66 days, and the range ran from under three weeks to most of a year.

quiz.q: You want to start flossing. Based on habit research, which approach is best?
options: Floss whenever you remember, at different times
Floss right after brushing your teeth every night
Floss only when you feel motivated
Floss intensely for 21 days, then stop paying attention
quiz.why: Repeating an action in the same context, linked to an existing routine, builds the cue-response link that makes it automatic.

entries.title: Ego depletion
entries.aka: Willpower as a muscle; the strength model of self-control
entries.line: The claim that using self-control drains a limited resource, weakening it for later tasks, has largely failed to replicate.
entries.idea: Ego depletion is the idea that self-control works like a muscle or a fuel tank. Each act of willpower, such as resisting a biscuit or holding back anger, uses up some of a limited supply. Afterwards you have less left, so you are more likely to give in to the next temptation. The idea was championed by Roy Baumeister and became hugely popular. It seemed to explain why we snack after a hard day and why tired people make poorer choices. Some researchers even claimed the resource was blood sugar, and that a sugary drink could top it up. Later, very large replication efforts, in which many labs repeated the same experiment, found little or no effect.

study.name: Radishes and cookies
study.who: Roy Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Mark Muraven and Dianne Tice
study.ref: Baumeister, R. F., Bratslavsky, E., Muraven, M., & Tice, D. M. (1998). Ego depletion: Is the active self a limited resource? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1252-1265.
study.story: Hungry students arrived at a psychology lab at Case Western Reserve University, having been asked to skip a meal. The room smelled wonderful. Chocolate chip cookies had just been baked there, and they sat on a table beside some chocolates. Next to them was a bowl of raw radishes. Some students were told to eat the cookies and chocolates. Others were told to eat only the radishes and leave the sweets alone. A third group was offered no food at all. The experimenter left the room, and the radish-eaters were secretly watched to check they did not sneak a cookie. None did, although some reportedly picked the cookies up and sniffed them. Then everyone moved on to what they were told was a separate task: a set of geometric puzzles. They were not told that the puzzles were impossible to solve. The real measure was how long each person kept trying before giving up. Students who had eaten the cookies, or nothing, kept going for around 20 minutes on average. Those who had made themselves eat radishes gave up after about eight minutes. Baumeister and his colleagues concluded that resisting the cookies had used up self-control, leaving less for the puzzles. The study inspired hundreds of follow-ups.
study.finding: Radish-eaters gave up on the impossible puzzles after about 8 minutes. The other two groups kept going for roughly 19 to 21 minutes.

entries.statusNote: Early meta-analyses (studies pooling many studies) seemed supportive. Later ones corrected for publication bias, where positive results are likelier to be published, and found little left. In 2016, a Registered Replication Report tested ego depletion in 23 labs with over 2,000 people. All labs ran the same preregistered plan (methods fixed in advance). The effect was close to zero. A second project in 2021 was led by Kathleen Vohs, an original proponent. It involved 36 labs and found at most a tiny effect. The blood sugar idea has also been undermined. Tiredness and boredom are real, but the strong 'limited resource' model has not held up.
life: Do not assume you are 'out of willpower' after one hard choice; believing it may matter more than any real drain.
Make self-control easier by shaping your surroundings, such as keeping snacks out of sight, rather than relying on reserves.
Be sceptical of products or diets that claim sugar boosts your self-control.
entries.myth: Myth: willpower is a fuel that runs low with every decision. Large replications found little evidence for this; fatigue and shifting motivation are real, but they are not a simple draining tank.

quiz.q: What did the large multi-lab replications of ego depletion find?
options: A large effect, bigger than the original
An effect close to zero
An effect only in people who eat sugar
An effect only for food temptations
quiz.why: When many labs ran the same preregistered study, the depletion effect was near zero, far smaller than the early results suggested.

entries.title: Growth mindset
entries.aka: Fixed versus growth mindset; implicit theories of intelligence
entries.line: Believing abilities can grow may help people persist, but school mindset programmes have mostly small, targeted effects.
entries.idea: Carol Dweck proposed that people hold beliefs about whether abilities are fixed or can develop. In a 'fixed mindset', talent is a set amount, so failure reveals a limit and needing effort signals weakness. In a 'growth mindset', abilities develop through effort, good strategies and help, so setbacks are part of learning. Dweck argued that growth-minded students seek challenges and bounce back from failure, while fixed-minded students avoid tests they might fail. The idea spread rapidly through schools and businesses, often in simplified form. Researchers also developed short online lessons teaching students that the brain grows stronger with practice. The key question is how much these beliefs, and these lessons, actually change results.

study.name: Praise for intelligence versus effort
study.ref: Mueller, C. M., & Dweck, C. S. (1998). Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(1), 33-52.
study.story: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck ran a series of studies with fifth-graders, children of about ten or eleven. Each child first worked on a set of moderately difficult reasoning puzzles. Whatever their actual score, every child was told they had done well. Then came a single sentence of praise that differed by group. Some heard, 'You must be smart at these problems.' Others heard, 'You must have worked hard at these problems.' A third group heard no extra comment. Next, the children were asked what kind of task they would like to try. Many of those praised for intelligence picked easy problems that would make them look clever. Most of those praised for effort picked harder problems they could learn from. Then every child faced a much harder set, on which nearly everyone did poorly. Afterwards, the children praised for intelligence enjoyed the puzzles less, wanted to keep going less and did worse on a final, easier set. When asked to report their scores to children at another school, more of them exaggerated. The children praised for effort stayed keener and recovered better. One sentence of praise, it seemed, could teach a child what failure meant.
study.finding: Compared with children praised for effort, those praised for intelligence chose easier tasks. They also enjoyed hard problems less and did worse after failure.

entries.statusNote: The picture is weaker than the popular story. A 2018 meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) by Victoria Sisk and colleagues found mindset only weakly linked to grades, and tiny average effects of mindset lessons. In 2019, a large, preregistered (methods fixed in advance) US study led by David Yeager appeared in Nature. A short online lesson modestly raised grades, mainly for lower-achieving students in supportive schools. Later meta-analyses disagree on whether any average effect survives. At least one attempt to repeat the praise result failed. Mindset may matter for some students in some settings.
life: When praising, comment on effort, strategy or progress ('you tried a new approach') rather than fixed traits ('you're a genius').
Pair 'you can improve' with real help: better strategies and support matter more than slogans.
Be cautious of costly mindset training sold as a cure-all; the measured effects are usually small.
entries.myth: Myth: simply teaching people a growth mindset transforms their results. The average effects of mindset lessons are small, and appear mainly for struggling students in supportive settings.

quiz.q: What does the best current evidence suggest about growth mindset lessons in schools?
options: They dramatically raise grades for all students
They have no effect on anyone
They have small effects, mostly for some struggling students in supportive settings
They work only when teachers praise intelligence
quiz.why: Large studies and meta-analyses find small, targeted effects rather than broad transformations.

entries.title: The marshmallow test
entries.line: Young children's ability to wait for a bigger treat predicts later outcomes far less once family background is considered.
entries.idea: The marshmallow test measures delay of gratification: the ability to wait for a bigger reward rather than take a smaller one now. A young child is offered one treat immediately, or two if they can wait alone until the adult returns. Walter Mischel first used it to study how children cope with temptation. Strategies mattered greatly. Children who distracted themselves, or thought about something fun, waited longer. The test became famous for a later claim. Children who waited longer at age four seemed, years later, to have higher test scores and better social skills. That turned a study of attention strategies into a popular symbol of self-control as destiny.

study.name: The Bing nursery studies
study.who: Walter Mischel, Ebbe Ebbesen and Antonette Zeiss
study.ref: Mischel, W., Ebbesen, E. B., & Zeiss, A. R. (1972). Cognitive and attentional mechanisms in delay of gratification. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 21(2), 204-218.
study.story: In the late 1960s and early 1970s, Walter Mischel and his colleagues ran a series of studies at the Bing Nursery School on the Stanford University campus. A child of about four or five was led into a small, plain room. On the table sat a treat, such as a marshmallow or a pretzel. The experimenter explained a deal. If the child could wait until the adult came back, they would get two treats. If they could not wait, they could ring a bell, and the adult would return at once, but they would get only one. Then the adult left. What happened next was often charming. Some children covered their eyes, turned their chairs around or sang to themselves. Others stared at the treat, stroked it or gave in within seconds. In one set of experiments, the researchers varied what the children were told to think about while waiting. Children encouraged to think 'fun thoughts', or given a toy to play with, could wait far longer. Children told to think about the treats gave in much sooner. Waiting depended on how attention was managed, not just on inner strength. Years later, Mischel's team contacted the families of former participants. Their reports suggested that longer waiters had become more successful teenagers, which made the test famous.
study.finding: Children waited much longer when they distracted themselves or thought about something fun. They gave in sooner when they focused on the rewards.

entries.statusNote: The original lab findings about distraction strategies hold up reasonably well. The famous long-term predictions hold up less well. The follow-ups involved small, mostly privileged samples from a university nursery. In 2018, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan repeated the analysis with a larger, more diverse group of around 900 children. The link with later achievement was about half as large. It shrank much further once they accounted for family background and early cognitive ability. Other work shows children wait less when adults have just proved unreliable, so waiting partly reflects trust.
life: Help children (and yourself) wait by changing focus: put the tempting thing out of sight or turn attention to something else.
If a child will not wait, consider whether they have reason to doubt the promise; trust shapes patience.
Be wary of anyone claiming a single childhood test reveals a person's destiny.
entries.myth: Myth: a four-year-old's marshmallow test result predicts their success in life. Much of the link reflects family background and early abilities, and it shrinks sharply when those are taken into account.

quiz.q: In Mischel's studies, what most helped young children wait for the larger reward?
options: Staring at the treat to build resolve
Being told the treat was very tasty
Distracting themselves or thinking about something fun
Being reminded how hungry they were
quiz.why: Shifting attention away from the treat made waiting much easier, showing that strategy mattered more than sheer grit.

entries.title: Flow
entries.aka: Being in the zone; optimal experience
entries.line: People often become deeply absorbed in tasks with clear goals and a challenge that roughly matches their skill.
entries.idea: Flow is the state of being completely absorbed in what you are doing. Time seems to vanish, self-consciousness fades and action feels effortless, even though you are working hard. The Hungarian-American psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi described it after interviewing rock climbers, chess players, surgeons and artists.
