He found that flow tends to appear under certain conditions. The task has clear goals and gives immediate feedback. Above all, its challenge roughly matches your skill. If the challenge is too low, you get bored. If it is too high, you get anxious. Flow can happen in sport, music, games, conversation or work. It is rewarding in itself, so people seek it out again and again.

study.name: The paradox of work
study.ref: Csikszentmihalyi, M., & LeFevre, J. (1989). Optimal experience in work and leisure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 56(5), 815-822.
study.story: How do you study a feeling while people are living it? Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi and Judith LeFevre used a method called experience sampling. They gave working adults in the Chicago area electronic pagers. For a week, each pager beeped at random moments during the day. At every beep, the person stopped and filled in a page of a short booklet. Where were they? What were they doing? How challenging was it, and how skilled did they feel? How happy, motivated and focused were they? This produced thousands of snapshots of ordinary life. The researchers classed a moment as flow when both challenge and skill were above that person's own average. The result was a puzzle. People were in flow far more often at work than in their free time. Leisure moments, often spent watching television or chatting, were mostly low in challenge and skill, a state the researchers called apathy. Yet when beeped at work, people often said they wished they were doing something else. When beeped during leisure, they were happier to be where they were. Flow moments felt good wherever they happened, but people did not seem to notice that their jobs gave them more of them. The authors called this the paradox of work.
study.finding: Workers reported flow more often at work than in leisure. Yet at work they were more likely to wish they were elsewhere.

entries.statusNote: Flow is well documented across cultures and activities, and measures of it predict enjoyment, wellbeing and performance. The weaker part is the precise rule. A 2015 meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) found that the balance of challenge and skill is linked to flow, but only moderately. Other factors, such as clear goals, interest and personality, also matter. Much of the evidence is correlational (showing links rather than proving cause) and self-reported. So the experience itself is real and robust, while 'challenge equals skill' is a useful guide rather than a law.
life: If a task bores you, raise the challenge with a time limit or a higher standard; if it overwhelms you, break it into smaller steps.
Protect blocks of uninterrupted time; notifications break flow quickly.
Notice that games and apps are designed to keep the challenge just above your skill, which is partly why they are hard to put down.
entries.myth: Myth: flow only happens to creative geniuses or elite athletes. Ordinary people report it often, including at work, during tasks with clear goals and the right level of challenge.

quiz.q: Your new job feels dull and easy. According to flow research, what would most likely bring on flow?
options: Taking more breaks
Raising the challenge to match your skills
Lowering your goals further
Doing several tasks at once
quiz.why: Flow is most likely when challenge rises to meet skill; low challenge with high skill tends to produce boredom.

entries.title: The Zeigarnik effect
entries.aka: Memory for unfinished tasks; the Ovsiankina effect (the urge to resume)
entries.line: Interrupted tasks were said to be remembered better than finished ones; modern evidence mainly supports an urge to resume them.
entries.idea: The Zeigarnik effect is the claim that we remember unfinished or interrupted tasks better than completed ones. The explanation came from Kurt Lewin's ideas about mental tension. Starting a task creates a kind of tension that lasts until the task is done. While the task is open, it stays active in the mind and easier to recall. Once it is finished, the tension is released and the memory fades. A related idea, named after Maria Ovsiankina, another of Lewin's students, is that people feel driven to go back and finish interrupted tasks. The Zeigarnik effect is popular in productivity advice and in television, where cliffhangers are said to keep a story nagging at you.

study.name: Completed and interrupted tasks
study.ref: Zeigarnik, B. (1927). Das Behalten erledigter und unerledigter Handlungen [The retention of completed and uncompleted actions]. Psychologische Forschung, 9, 1-85.
study.story: The story goes that Kurt Lewin, a psychologist in 1920s Berlin, sat in a café with his students. A waiter took a large order without writing anything down and served it perfectly. Later, someone asked him what they had ordered. He could not remember. Once the bill was settled, the order seemed to have vanished from his mind. Whether or not it happened exactly like that, it inspired a young student, Bluma Zeigarnik, to test the idea. She gave adults and children a series of around twenty short tasks. They made clay figures, solved puzzles, strung beads and did simple sums. Some tasks she allowed them to finish. Others she interrupted before they could complete them, by moving them on to the next one. The participants were not told that their memory would be tested. At the end, she asked them to list all the tasks they could remember. On average, people recalled the interrupted tasks considerably more often than the completed ones, by her account nearly twice as often. The effect seemed strongest in people who were keen and ambitious about the tasks. Zeigarnik concluded that unfinished business stays alive in the mind. The finding went on to appear in textbooks, sales training and screenwriting guides.
study.finding: Participants recalled interrupted tasks more often than completed ones. She reported a ratio close to two to one.

entries.statusNote: Later attempts to repeat Zeigarnik's memory result were inconsistent. Some found the effect, some found none and some found the reverse. Results depended on details, such as whether people felt that being interrupted meant they had failed. A meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) published in 2025 concluded that there is no reliable general memory advantage for unfinished tasks. However, the urge to resume interrupted tasks, the Ovsiankina effect, did hold up. So unfinished tasks do tug at us, but not necessarily by being better remembered.
life: If unfinished work keeps nagging at you in the evening, write down your next step; that often eases the pull.
To restart a stalled project easily, stop work mid-task so you feel drawn back to it the next day.
Spot the trick in cliffhangers and 'next episode' countdowns: they exploit your urge to finish what you started.
entries.myth: Myth: we reliably remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones. The memory effect is inconsistent; what holds up better is our urge to go back and complete them.

quiz.q: What does modern evidence most support about interrupted tasks?
options: They are always remembered about twice as well
People tend to feel drawn to resume them
They are always forgotten faster
They have no psychological effects at all
quiz.why: Recent reviews find the memory advantage unreliable, but the tendency to go back and finish interrupted tasks holds up.

entries.title: Learned helplessness
entries.line: After repeated uncontrollable bad events, animals and people often stop trying to escape, even when escape becomes possible.
entries.idea: Learned helplessness describes giving up after repeated experiences of having no control. If nothing you do changes what happens, you may stop trying, even later when your actions could help. Martin Seligman and Steven Maier first described this in dogs in the 1960s. They proposed that the animals had learned that their actions did not matter. The idea was soon applied to people and became an influential model of depression. A later version stressed how people explain bad events. Seeing setbacks as permanent, all-pervading and entirely your own fault seemed to deepen helplessness. Decades later, brain research led Maier and Seligman to revise the core idea: passivity may be the default, and what is learned is control.

study.name: Failure to escape
study.ref: Seligman, M. E. P., & Maier, S. F. (1967). Failure to escape traumatic shock. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 74(1), 1-9.
study.story: At the University of Pennsylvania in the mid-1960s, Martin Seligman and Steven Maier ran experiments that would struggle to win approval today. Dogs were placed in harnesses and given electric shocks that were painful but not physically harmful. The design used three groups. Dogs in the first group could stop the shocks by pressing a panel with their heads. Dogs in the second group were 'yoked' to the first: each received exactly the same shocks at the same moments, but nothing it did made any difference. A third group received no shocks. A day later, each dog was put in a shuttle box, a box divided in two by a low barrier. When a shock came through the floor, the dog could escape simply by jumping over the barrier. Dogs from the first and third groups quickly learned to jump. Many dogs from the second group did something else. They lay down and endured the shocks, making little attempt to escape. Some that escaped once by chance failed to do so again. Pain alone could not explain this, because both shocked groups had received exactly the same amount. The difference was control. The researchers called it learned helplessness.
study.finding: Most dogs that had received uncontrollable shocks later failed to learn to escape. Dogs given controllable shocks, or none, learned quickly.

entries.statusNote: The basic animal finding has been repeated many times: uncontrollable stress produces passivity. But the explanation has been turned on its head. In a 2016 review, Maier and Seligman concluded from brain research that passivity is the default response to prolonged bad events. What animals learn, through a circuit in the prefrontal cortex, is that they have control. In humans, helplessness experiments using unsolvable puzzles show smaller, less consistent effects. The theory shaped depression research, but depression is now seen as having many causes. So the phenomenon is real, while the original story was wrong.
life: If someone has 'given up', look for situations where small actions visibly work; regaining control can restore effort.
When you face a setback, ask whether it is truly permanent and total; such explanations can feed giving up.
Notice systems that make effort feel pointless, like endless customer-service loops; they can train people into passivity.
entries.myth: Myth: helplessness is something people have to learn. Brain research now suggests passivity is the default under prolonged stress, and what has to be learned is that you have some control.

quiz.q: In the dog experiments, what caused the later failure to escape?
options: The amount of pain received
Having had no control over the earlier shocks
Tiredness from the harness
Never having seen a shuttle box
quiz.why: Both shocked groups got identical shocks; only the dogs that had no control later failed to escape.

entries.title: Deliberate practice
entries.line: Focused, effortful practice with feedback builds expertise, but it explains only part of why some people become better than others.
entries.idea: Deliberate practice is a particular kind of training. It is not just repetition, or playing for fun. It means working on specific weaknesses, at the edge of your ability, with clear goals and quick feedback, often guided by a teacher. Anders Ericsson argued that this kind of practice, built up over many years, is the main thing that separates experts from everyone else. On his view, talent matters far less than most people think. The writer Malcolm Gladwell later popularised the idea as the '10,000-hour rule', the claim that roughly that much practice makes anyone an expert. Ericsson himself objected that the figure was an average from one study, not a magic threshold.

study.name: The Berlin violinists
study.who: K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer
study.ref: Ericsson, K. A., Krampe, R. T., & Tesch-Römer, C. (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review, 100(3), 363-406.
study.story: In the late 1980s, Anders Ericsson and his colleagues visited a renowned music academy in West Berlin. They asked the professors to name the violin students most likely to become international soloists. They also identified a group of good violinists, and a group from a separate programme training to become music teachers. Each student was interviewed at length about their musical life. When had they started? How many hours a week had they practised alone at each age? For a week, they also kept a diary of everything they did, from lessons to sleep. All three groups agreed that practising alone was the most important activity for improving. They also agreed it was among the least enjoyable. The big differences lay in how much of it they had done. By the age of eighteen, the best violinists estimated that they had built up roughly 7,000 hours of solo practice. The future music teachers estimated only around 3,000 to 4,000. The researchers projected that the best group would pass 10,000 hours by the age of twenty. Interestingly, the best students also slept more, including afternoon naps. Ericsson concluded that expertise is built through years of effortful practice, not simply born.
study.finding: The best violinists reported far more solo practice than less accomplished peers. Their total was projected to reach around 10,000 hours by age twenty.

entries.statusNote: Practice clearly matters, but not as much as Ericsson claimed. In 2014, Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald ran a meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies). Deliberate practice explained about a fifth to a quarter of the differences in performance in games and music. It explained less in sport, and very little in education and professions. A 2019 repeat of the violin study found that the best violinists had not practised more than the merely good ones. Starting age, genes, working memory and personality also matter. Ericsson disputed how these analyses defined deliberate practice.
life: Practise the hard parts, not the bits you already do well, and get quick feedback from a coach, a recording or a test.
Short, focused sessions with rest beat long, distracted hours; the Berlin violinists also slept well.
Be wary of '10,000 hours' promises: practice helps everyone improve, but it does not guarantee a world-class level.
entries.myth: Myth: 10,000 hours of practice makes anyone an expert. That figure was an average from one study of violinists, and practice explains only part of the differences between people.

quiz.q: Which of these best describes deliberate practice?
options: Repeating a piece you already play well, for enjoyment
Working on specific weaknesses with clear goals and feedback
Practising for exactly 10,000 hours
Watching experts perform
quiz.why: Deliberate practice targets the edge of your ability with goals and feedback, unlike simple repetition.

entries.title: The two-factor theory of emotion
entries.aka: Schachter-Singer theory; arousal plus a label
entries.line: Emotion was proposed to be bodily arousal plus a mental label taken from the situation; the original evidence proved weak.
entries.idea: The two-factor theory, proposed by Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer, says an emotion needs two ingredients. The first is physical arousal: a racing heart, sweaty palms, fast breathing. The second is a cognitive label, an explanation of why you feel stirred up. On this view, arousal itself is much the same across emotions. What makes it fear, anger or joy is how you interpret it, usually from clues around you. If you feel aroused but have no obvious explanation, you search the situation for one. That opened the door to 'misattribution', mistaking the source of your arousal. The theory helped launch the modern idea that how we interpret events shapes what we feel.

study.name: The Suproxin experiment
study.ref: Schachter, S., & Singer, J. E. (1962). Cognitive, social, and physiological determinants of emotional state. Psychological Review, 69(5), 379-399.
study.story: Male students at the University of Minnesota volunteered for what they thought was a study of a vitamin called 'Suproxin' and its effects on vision. In fact, most were injected with adrenaline (epinephrine), which raises heart rate and can cause trembling and flushing. Some were told accurately which side effects to expect. Others were told nothing, or were misinformed. A comparison group received a harmless salt-water injection. Each student then waited in a room with another 'volunteer', who was really an actor working for the researchers. In one version, the actor was euphoric. He made paper planes, threw screwed-up paper at a wastebasket and played with a hula hoop. In another, he and the student filled in a long questionnaire that grew more and more insulting, including personal questions about their families. The actor grew angry, tore up his questionnaire and stormed out. Observers behind a one-way mirror recorded what the student did. Schachter and Singer predicted that students with unexplained arousal would 'catch' the actor's mood, while those who knew what the injection did would not. Some results fitted, especially in the euphoric version. Uninformed students tended to join in more and report feeling happier than informed ones. But many differences were small, and the salt-water group often did not behave as predicted.
study.finding: Uninformed students given adrenaline showed somewhat more of the actor's mood than informed students. But many differences were small and inconsistent.

entries.statusNote: The key results did not replicate well: when other researchers repeated the study, they got different results. In 1979, Gary Marshall and Philip Zimbardo, and separately Christina Maslach, tried similar procedures. They found that unexplained arousal tended to feel unpleasant, rather than taking on whatever mood was around. A 1983 review by Rainer Reisenzein concluded that arousal can intensify emotions and can sometimes be misattributed. But it found little evidence that arousal plus a label is either necessary or sufficient for emotion. The broader idea, that interpretation shapes emotion, lives on in modern theories.
life: If you feel jittery after coffee or exercise, remember why before deciding that you are anxious or angry.
Before reacting to a strong feeling, ask what else might explain your racing heart: tiredness, caffeine, heat.
Notice how loud music and fast editing in adverts or rallies stir up arousal that then gets pinned to a product or cause.
entries.myth: Myth: every emotion is just generic arousal with a label, so you can feel anything if you relabel it. Arousal and interpretation do interact, but the evidence for this strong claim was weak.

quiz.q: According to the two-factor theory, what turns physical arousal into a specific emotion?
options: The amount of adrenaline in the blood
How you interpret the arousal, using clues from the situation
Which facial muscles are active
How long the arousal lasts
quiz.why: The theory holds that arousal is fairly general and that the label you give it, from context, makes it a particular emotion.

entries.title: Affect labelling
entries.aka: Name it to tame it; putting feelings into words
entries.line: Putting a feeling into words can lower its intensity, even though people rarely expect it to help.
entries.idea: Affect labelling means naming an emotion, either one you feel or one you see: 'I feel anxious' or 'that face looks angry'. It sounds too simple to matter. Yet studies suggest that labelling can take the edge off strong feelings. In brain scans, naming the emotion shown in a face reduced activity in the amygdala, a brain region involved in detecting threats. It also increased activity in a part of the prefrontal cortex linked with calming emotions down. Unlike reappraisal, you do not need to change how you see the situation. You only need to put the feeling into words. Researchers think labelling may work as a kind of unintentional emotion regulation.

study.name: Putting feelings into words
study.who: Matthew Lieberman, Naomi Eisenberger, Molly Crockett, Sabrina Tom, Jennifer Pfeifer and Baldwin Way
study.ref: Lieberman, M. D., Eisenberger, N. I., Crockett, M. J., Tom, S. M., Pfeifer, J. H., & Way, B. M. (2007). Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli. Psychological Science, 18(5), 421-428.
study.story: Matthew Lieberman and his colleagues at the University of California, Los Angeles asked volunteers to lie in a brain scanner and look at a series of photographs of faces. Each face showed a strong emotion, such as anger or fear. Below the face, two choices appeared, and the volunteer pressed a button to pick one. In some trials, the choices were emotion words, such as 'angry' and 'scared'. The volunteer had to name the feeling shown. In other trials, the choices were two first names, such as 'Harry' and 'Sally', and they had to pick the name that fitted the face's sex. In still others, they matched the face to another face showing the same emotion, without naming it. All these tasks involved looking closely at emotional faces. The difference was whether words for feelings were used. The scans showed that the amygdala, which usually responds strongly to fearful and angry faces, was less active when people named the emotion. At the same time, a region in the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, behind the temple, became more active. The more active that region was, the quieter the amygdala tended to be. Simply attaching a word to a feeling, it seemed, turned the alarm down a notch.
study.finding: Naming the emotion in a face reduced amygdala activity compared with the other tasks. It also increased activity in a right prefrontal region linked to calming emotions.

entries.statusNote: The idea has reasonable support. Several brain-imaging studies and behavioural experiments find that labelling feelings lowers distress, physical arousal or amygdala activity. A 2012 study of people afraid of spiders found that describing their feelings during exposure to a spider reduced their physical fear response a week later. But many studies are small, brain-imaging samples are often tiny, and large preregistered tests (with methods fixed in advance) are scarce. Effects on how people say they feel tend to be modest. It is promising, but needs bigger, more rigorous replications.
life: When upset, try naming the feeling precisely ('I'm frustrated and embarrassed') rather than pushing it away.
With a distressed child, calmly naming their feeling ('you're really disappointed') can help them settle.
Journaling or telling a friend how you feel may help partly through the simple act of naming.
entries.myth: Myth: talking about a bad feeling just makes it worse by dwelling on it. Briefly naming a feeling often softens it; endless rumination is a different thing.

quiz.q: In the brain-scanning study, which task reduced amygdala activity most?
options: Matching a face to another with the same emotion
Choosing a word that names the emotion shown
Picking a name that fits the face's sex
Looking at the face without doing anything
quiz.why: Naming the emotion in words was what quietened the amygdala, compared with tasks that only involved looking at emotional faces.

entries.title: Cognitive reappraisal
entries.line: Changing how you interpret a situation usually reduces negative feelings more effectively than hiding them.
entries.idea: Cognitive reappraisal means changing the way you think about a situation in order to change how you feel about it. Imagine a colleague ignores you in the corridor. You could think 'she's snubbing me', or 'she looks distracted, maybe she's had bad news'. The second thought takes the sting out. James Gross, a leading emotion researcher, contrasts reappraisal with suppression, which means keeping a straight face and hiding what you feel. Reappraisal works early, before the emotion has fully taken hold. Suppression works late, after the feeling is already there. Reappraisal is a core skill in cognitive behavioural therapy. It is not pretending everything is fine. It means finding an interpretation that is realistic and also less distressing.

study.name: The disgust film study
study.ref: Gross, J. J. (1998). Antecedent- and response-focused emotion regulation: Divergent consequences for experience, expression, and physiology. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(1), 224-237.
study.story: James Gross, then at Stanford University, showed volunteers a short and unpleasant film. It showed medical scenes, including the treatment of a burn victim and an arm amputation, that most people find disgusting. Before watching, the volunteers were divided into three groups. One group was asked to reappraise. They were to watch with a detached, clinical attitude, as if they were medical professionals studying the procedure. A second group was asked to suppress. They were to hide their feelings, so that anyone watching them would not know what they felt. A third group was simply asked to watch. While the film played, a hidden camera recorded their faces, and sensors tracked their heart and skin responses. Afterwards they rated how disgusted they had felt. Both strategies changed what showed on the face: both groups looked less disgusted than the plain watchers. Inside, though, they differed. The reappraisers also reported feeling less disgust. The suppressors felt about as disgusted as the plain watchers. Their bodies also showed signs of extra strain, with more activity in the sympathetic nervous system, the body's 'fight or flight' system. Hiding the feeling took effort without making it go away. Changing how they saw the scene did both.
study.finding: Reappraisal reduced both felt disgust and its visible expression. Suppression reduced expression only, and increased signs of physical stress.

entries.statusNote: Reappraisal is one of the better-supported findings in emotion research. A 2012 meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) by Thomas Webb, Eleanor Miles and Paschal Sheeran combined hundreds of experimental comparisons. It found reappraisal had small to moderate effects on how people felt, while suppressing expressions did little for feelings. Studies of daily life link habitual reappraisal with better wellbeing. There are caveats. It is harder under intense stress, it suits some situations better than others, and where you can change a situation, solving the problem may beat reframing it.
life: When something stings, ask 'What is another plausible explanation?' and choose the most realistic, kinder one.
Before a nerve-racking event, try seeing it as a challenge or a chance to practise rather than a test of your worth.
Do not use reframing to tolerate things you should change, such as mistreatment; sometimes action beats reinterpretation.
entries.myth: Myth: bottling up emotions and keeping a brave face is the same as managing them. Hiding a feeling usually leaves it intact inside, while reappraisal changes the feeling itself.

quiz.q: In Gross's disgust film study, what did suppression achieve compared with reappraisal?
options: It reduced felt disgust more
It reduced visible expression but not felt disgust
It had no effect at all
It lowered heart and stress responses
quiz.why: Suppressors looked less disgusted but felt the same and showed extra physical strain; reappraisers also felt less disgust.

entries.title: The facial feedback hypothesis
entries.line: Moving your face into a smile may nudge your mood slightly, but the famous pen-in-mouth result did not replicate.
entries.idea: The facial feedback hypothesis says your facial expressions do not only show your emotions. They also feed back into them. Smile, and you may feel a little happier; frown, and you may feel a little worse. The idea goes back to Charles Darwin and William James. It comes in strong and weak versions. The strong version says expressions are needed to feel emotions at all. The weak version says they can slightly intensify or shape feelings. A famous test used a pen held in the mouth to tense the smiling muscles without people realising. It was designed so participants would not guess what was being studied, and it became a textbook classic.

study.name: The pen in the mouth
study.who: Fritz Strack, Leonard Martin and Sabine Stepper
study.ref: Strack, F., Martin, L. L., & Stepper, S. (1988). Inhibiting and facilitating conditions of the human smile: A nonobtrusive test of the facial feedback hypothesis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(5), 768-777.
study.story: Fritz Strack, Leonard Martin and Sabine Stepper needed a way to make people smile without knowing it. If you simply asked people to smile, they might guess the point and play along. So the researchers invented a cover story. Participants were told the study was about how people who cannot use their hands might learn to do tasks with their mouths. Some held a pen between their teeth, without letting their lips touch it. This pulls the face into something like a smile. Others held the pen with their lips only, which makes smiling difficult and produces something closer to a pout. A third group held the pen in their non-dominant hand. While holding the pen, participants did several small tasks, such as drawing lines between numbers. Then came the key one. They rated how funny they found a set of cartoons from Gary Larson's 'The Far Side'. People holding the pen in their teeth rated the cartoons somewhat funnier than those holding it in their lips. The difference was modest, but it suggested something remarkable. A smile they did not know they were making had made the jokes seem funnier. The study became a staple of textbooks and was cited thousands of times.
study.finding: Participants holding a pen in their teeth rated the cartoons as somewhat funnier than those holding it in their lips.

entries.statusNote: In 2016, a Registered Replication Report ran the pen study in 17 labs with nearly 1,900 participants. All the labs followed one preregistered plan (methods fixed in advance). It found no effect. Some argued that filming participants, as the replications did, may have mattered. A 2019 meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) of nearly 140 studies found a small overall facial feedback effect. In 2022, the Many Smiles Collaboration tested nearly 3,900 people in 19 countries. Copying or posing a smile raised happiness slightly, but the pen method did not.
life: A deliberate smile might give your mood a small lift, but do not expect it to rescue a bad day.
Do not tell someone who is upset to 'just smile'; the effect is small and the pressure can backfire.
Notice that laughter tracks and smiling presenters may lift your mood partly by inviting you to smile along.
entries.myth: Myth: holding a pen in your teeth will make you happier. That classic result failed in a 17-lab replication; posed smiles have at most a small effect on mood.

quiz.q: What did the large 2022 Many Smiles study find?
options: The pen-in-mouth method strongly improved mood
Posed smiles raised happiness slightly, but the pen method did not
Facial expressions have no link to feelings at all
Only frowning affects mood
quiz.why: Posing or copying a smile slightly raised happiness, while the pen method showed no reliable effect.

entries.title: Power posing
entries.line: Expansive 'power poses' were said to change hormones and boldness; these effects failed to replicate.
entries.idea: Power posing is the idea that standing or sitting in an expansive, open posture, such as hands on hips or feet on the desk, changes how you feel and act, not just how you look. A 2010 study claimed that holding such poses for two minutes raised testosterone, lowered the stress hormone cortisol and made people more willing to take risks. Amy Cuddy, one of the authors, presented the idea in a 2012 TED talk that became one of the most watched ever. The message was empowering: before a job interview, strike a confident pose in private. Then the evidence began to crumble, and the case became a central story in psychology's replication crisis.

study.name: Two minutes of power
study.who: Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap
study.ref: Carney, D. R., Cuddy, A. J. C., & Yap, A. J. (2010). Power posing: Brief nonverbal displays affect neuroendocrine levels and risk tolerance. Psychological Science, 21(10), 1363-1368.
study.story: Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap brought 42 people into a lab. To explain the odd postures they would be asked to hold, participants were told the study was about where heart sensors should be placed on the body. Each person first gave a saliva sample, which can be tested for hormones. Then the experimenter arranged them into two poses, held for one minute each. Half took high-power poses: leaning back with feet on a desk and hands behind the head, or standing and leaning over a table with hands spread wide. The other half took low-power poses: sitting hunched with hands in the lap, or standing with arms and legs tightly crossed. Next, each participant was given two dollars and offered a gamble. They could keep the money, or roll a die for an even chance of doubling it or losing it. Then they rated how powerful and in charge they felt, and gave a second saliva sample. The results looked striking. High-power posers reported feeling more powerful and were more likely to take the gamble. Their testosterone rose and their cortisol fell, while the low-power posers showed the reverse. Two minutes of posture, it seemed, could reshape body chemistry.
study.finding: High-power posers felt more powerful and gambled more often (86 per cent versus 60 per cent). They also showed higher testosterone and lower cortisol.

entries.statusNote: In 2015, Eva Ranehill and colleagues repeated the study with about 200 participants. They found no effects on hormones or risk-taking, only a small rise in feeling powerful. In 2016, Dana Carney, the original first author, publicly stated that she no longer believed power posing effects are real. Cuddy and colleagues later argued that the evidence supports an effect on feelings of power. Later preregistered studies (with methods fixed in advance) and reviews suggest any effect on feelings is small, while claims about hormones and behaviour lack support. The headline claims have failed.
life: If an open posture helps you feel a little more confident before an interview, it is harmless, but expect no hormonal boost.
Prepare your content and practise your answers; those matter far more than posture.
Be wary of life hacks resting on one small study with a famous talk behind it.
entries.myth: Myth: two minutes of power posing boosts testosterone and boldness. Large replications found no effects on hormones or risk-taking; at most, people feel slightly more powerful.

quiz.q: What survives of the power posing claims after replications?
options: Large rises in testosterone
More risk-taking in gambles
At most a small increase in feeling powerful
Lower cortisol before interviews
quiz.why: Replications found no hormonal or behavioural effects; only a small effect on feelings of power has some support.

entries.title: The Yerkes-Dodson law
entries.line: Performance is said to peak at moderate arousal, but the original 1908 mouse study tested something much narrower.
entries.idea: The Yerkes-Dodson law is usually drawn as an upside-down U. As arousal or stress rises, performance improves, up to a point. Beyond that, more arousal makes performance worse. The peak is said to come earlier for difficult tasks than for easy ones. So a little nervousness helps you give a talk, but panic ruins it, and a complex task needs a calmer state than a simple one. It is one of the most widely quoted ideas in psychology, from sports coaching to management courses. Yet the original study did not measure arousal at all. It measured how quickly mice learned a task when given electric shocks of different strengths.

study.name: The dancing mice
study.ref: Yerkes, R. M., & Dodson, J. D. (1908). The relation of strength of stimulus to rapidity of habit-formation. Journal of Comparative Neurology and Psychology, 18(5), 459-482.
study.story: At Harvard in the early 1900s, Robert Yerkes and his student John Dodson worked with 'dancing mice', a strain known for spinning in circles. They built a box in which each mouse had to choose between two compartments, one white and one black. The mice had to learn to choose the white one. Each time a mouse went towards the black side, it received an electric shock. The researchers varied two things. The first was the strength of the shock, from weak to strong. The second was the difficulty of the task, made easier or harder by changing how clearly the two compartments could be told apart. They counted how many trials each mouse needed before it reliably chose correctly. When the choice was easy, stronger shocks led to faster learning. When it was hard, the mice learned fastest with medium shocks, and strong shocks slowed them down. The researchers concluded that the best level of stimulation depends on the difficulty of the task. Each condition used only a small number of mice. For decades the paper was rarely cited. Only in the 1950s, when psychologists became interested in arousal, was it rediscovered and recast as a general law about arousal and performance.
study.finding: With an easy choice, stronger shocks sped up learning. With a hard one, medium shocks worked best and strong shocks slowed learning down.

entries.statusNote: The original study was small, and it measured learning under shocks rather than arousal. Its results did not show a clean inverted U in every condition. The idea was later stretched into a general law about arousal, stress and performance. Reviews, such as one by Karl Halvor Teigen in 1994, have shown how much the 'law' changed as it was retold. Modern research does find some inverted-U patterns, for example between stress hormones and memory. But arousal is hard to define and measure, and many studies find simpler patterns. It is a useful rule of thumb, not a law.
life: If you feel flat before a big task, a little energy (music, a brisk walk) may help; if you feel panicky, calm down first.
For complex or new tasks, aim for a calmer state than for simple, well-practised ones.
Be sceptical when a neat curve is used to justify putting people under pressure 'for their own good'.
entries.myth: Myth: Yerkes and Dodson proved that moderate stress is best for performance. Their study was about mice learning under electric shocks; the arousal 'law' was built on it decades later.

quiz.q: What did the original 1908 Yerkes-Dodson study actually measure?
options: How stress affects students' exam scores
How fast mice learned a choice under shocks of different strengths
Heart rate during public speaking
Arousal levels in athletes
quiz.why: The study measured mice learning to choose a compartment under shocks of varying strength; it was later reinterpreted as being about arousal.

entries.title: Hedonic adaptation
entries.line: People tend to get used to good and bad changes in their lives, though adaptation is often incomplete.
entries.idea: Hedonic adaptation is our tendency to get used to changes in our lives, so that their emotional impact fades. A pay rise, a new car or a new home brings a lift, but after a while it becomes normal and our happiness drifts back. The same can happen after some bad events. The process is sometimes called the 'hedonic treadmill': we keep running for more, but our happiness stays roughly in place. Adaptation is partly a good thing, because it helps us recover from setbacks. But it also explains why gains rarely deliver lasting joy. People typically underestimate how much they will adapt, so they overpredict how much future events will affect them.

study.name: Lottery winners and accident victims
study.who: Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman
study.ref: Brickman, P., Coates, D., & Janoff-Bulman, R. (1978). Lottery winners and accident victims: Is happiness relative? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 36(8), 917-927.
study.story: Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman wanted to test a striking prediction. If people adapt to good fortune, then even a big lottery win should not leave them much happier. They interviewed 22 people in Illinois who had won large sums in the state lottery, from tens of thousands of dollars up to a million. They compared them with ordinary people living in the same areas. They also interviewed people who had recently been paralysed in accidents, some unable to use their legs and some unable to use their arms and legs. Everyone rated how happy they were now, how happy they had been before and how happy they expected to be in a couple of years. They also rated how much they enjoyed everyday pleasures, such as chatting with a friend, watching television or hearing a joke. The lottery winners were not significantly happier than the comparison group, meaning the difference was too small to rule out chance. They also reported getting less pleasure from everyday activities, as if the win had dulled ordinary joys. The accident victims rated themselves less happy than the others, but still above the middle of the scale. They also looked back on their past with nostalgia. The study became the classic illustration of the hedonic treadmill.
study.finding: Lottery winners were not much happier than their neighbours, and enjoyed everyday pleasures less. Accident victims were less happy, but still above the scale's midpoint.

entries.statusNote: Adaptation is real, but often less complete than the classic study suggested. That study was small and took a single snapshot in time. Richard Lucas and others analysed large studies that followed thousands of people for years. Many people did not fully return to their earlier wellbeing after disability, unemployment or losing a partner. A 2020 study of Swedish lottery players found that large wins raised life satisfaction for more than a decade. People do adapt, but some changes leave lasting marks, for better and for worse.
life: Spend on experiences and variety rather than one big purchase; varied pleasures tend to fade more slowly.
Before a major purchase, remember that the thrill will probably fade within months.
After a setback, take comfort that most people recover more than they expect, but seek help if low mood lingers.
entries.myth: Myth: winning the lottery makes no difference to happiness. Newer, larger studies find that big wins raise life satisfaction for years; adaptation is real but not total.

quiz.q: Why do people often overestimate how long a new car will make them happy?
options: Cars lose value quickly
They underestimate how quickly they will get used to it
Happiness never changes
They soon forget they bought it
quiz.why: Hedonic adaptation makes new things feel normal, and people tend not to foresee this.

entries.title: The negativity bias
entries.line: Bad events, feedback and information tend to affect us more strongly than good ones of similar size.
entries.idea: The negativity bias is the tendency for negative things to grab our attention and affect us more than positive things of the same size. One criticism can sting more than several compliments please. A single bad review can outweigh many good ones. Losing a sum of money often feels worse than gaining the same sum feels good. Bad first impressions are also harder to undo than good ones. Two influential reviews in 2001, one by Roy Baumeister and colleagues and one by Paul Rozin and Edward Royzman, gathered evidence from many areas of life. A common explanation is evolutionary. For our ancestors, missing a threat could be fatal, while missing an opportunity usually was not.

study.name: Negative pictures in the brain
study.who: Tiffany Ito, Jeff Larsen, Kyle Smith and John Cacioppo
study.ref: Ito, T. A., Larsen, J. T., Smith, N. K., & Cacioppo, J. T. (1998). Negative information weighs more heavily on the brain: The negativity bias in evaluative categorizations. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(4), 887-900.
study.story: Tiffany Ito, John Cacioppo and their colleagues at Ohio State University wanted to know whether the negativity bias shows up in the brain's earliest reactions. Volunteers wore a cap of electrodes that recorded the brain's electrical activity, measured to the millisecond. On a screen, they watched a stream of photographs, shown one after another. Most pictures were neutral, such as everyday household objects. Every so often, a pleasant picture appeared, such as appetising food or a cheerful scene. At other times, an unpleasant one appeared, such as an injured body or a dead animal. The volunteers simply pressed buttons to sort each picture. The researchers had chosen the pleasant and unpleasant pictures carefully. People rated them as equally extreme and equally arousing. That way, any difference in brain response could not simply be because the bad pictures were more shocking. The team focused on a brainwave that appears a few hundred milliseconds after an unexpected image. Its size is known to reflect how strongly the brain is evaluating what it sees. The unpleasant pictures produced larger brainwaves than the pleasant ones. Within a fraction of a second, before any deliberate thought, the brain seemed to weigh the bad more heavily than the good.
study.finding: Unpleasant pictures produced larger brain responses than pleasant ones. This held even though the two sets were matched for how extreme and arousing they were.

entries.statusNote: The general pattern is well supported in many areas, from impressions and relationships to news and money. But it is not universal. Some studies find that positive information gets more attention in certain settings. Older adults often show a 'positivity effect', attending more to good things. Feelings attached to bad memories also tend to fade faster than those attached to good ones. Some researchers argue the bias has been overstated, or depends heavily on how 'equal' good and bad are defined. Overall, the core finding holds, with real exceptions.
life: When giving feedback, remember that one harsh comment can outweigh several kind ones, and balance accordingly.
Recognise that news and social media lean on bad news partly because it grabs attention more.
Deliberately note good things each day, since they slip past more easily than bad ones.
entries.myth: Myth: the negativity bias means we are doomed to pessimism, with a fixed number of positives needed to cancel each negative. The bias is real, but precise magic ratios are not well established, and people also show positive biases.

quiz.q: Why did Ito and colleagues match the pleasant and unpleasant pictures for how extreme and arousing they were?
options: To make the task easier for volunteers
So that any difference could not be due to the bad pictures simply being more intense
To reduce the number of participants needed
Because pleasant pictures are rarer
quiz.why: Matching ruled out the explanation that the negative images were just stronger, isolating the effect of good versus bad.

entries.title: Expressive writing
entries.aka: The Pennebaker method; writing about upsetting experiences
entries.line: Writing about your deepest thoughts and feelings for a few days can bring small benefits to health and mood.
entries.idea: Expressive writing is a simple exercise developed by James Pennebaker. You write about your deepest thoughts and feelings about a stressful or upsetting experience. Typically, you write for 15 to 20 minutes on three or four days in a row. You need not worry about spelling or grammar, and nobody else needs to read it. Pennebaker first thought it worked by releasing bottled-up emotion. Later he suggested that turning experience into words helps people make sense of it and build a story about what happened. People whose writing shifted towards more insight and more 'because' words seemed to benefit most. The exercise often feels worse at first, but benefits seemed to appear in the following weeks and months.

study.name: Writing about trauma
study.ref: Pennebaker, J. W., & Beall, S. K. (1986). Confronting a traumatic event: Toward an understanding of inhibition and disease. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 95(3), 274-281.
study.story: James Pennebaker and Sandra Beall, at Southern Methodist University in Texas, asked students to come to a lab on four nights in a row. Each night, alone in a small room, they would write for 15 minutes. What they wrote about depended on their group. Some wrote about trivial topics, such as describing their room or their shoes. Others wrote about the most traumatic or upsetting experience of their lives. Within this second group, some were asked to write only the facts of what had happened. Some wrote only about their emotions. And some wrote about both the facts and their deepest feelings. Many students wrote about painful experiences, such as a death in the family, their parents' divorce, abuse or loneliness. Right after writing about trauma, they often felt worse. But months later, the picture had changed. The researchers checked the university health centre records. Students who had written about both the facts and their feelings had made fewer visits for illness in the following months than those who wrote about trivial topics. Writing only the facts, or only venting feelings, did not show the same clear benefit. Something about putting events and emotions together on paper seemed to matter.
study.finding: Some students wrote about both the facts and the feelings of a trauma. Over the following months, they made fewer illness visits to the health centre.

entries.statusNote: The effect is real but small. In 2006, Joanne Frattaroli ran a meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) of 146 studies. She found a small overall benefit, with large variation between studies. Other reviews have found small or no effects for particular groups, such as people with post-traumatic stress, depression or physical illness. Effects may be larger when people write about unresolved experiences, and in longer sessions. It is cheap and usually harmless. But it is no replacement for therapy, and it may not suit someone straight after a fresh trauma.
life: If a worry or upset keeps circling, try writing about both what happened and how you feel, for 15 minutes on a few days.
Expect to feel a bit worse straight afterwards; that is common and usually passes.
Do not use it as a substitute for professional help with serious distress or a recent trauma.
entries.myth: Myth: writing about trauma is a powerful cure. The average benefit is small, and simply venting emotions without making sense of events seems to help less.

quiz.q: In Pennebaker and Beall's study, which group later made the fewest health centre visits?
options: Those who wrote about trivial topics
Those who wrote only the facts of a trauma
Those who wrote about both the facts and their feelings
Those who wrote only about their feelings
quiz.why: Combining the facts with deep feelings, rather than either alone, was linked to fewer illness visits.

entries.title: Emotional contagion
entries.line: Moods can spread between people through mimicry and shared cues, although large-scale effects are usually small.
entries.idea: Emotional contagion is the tendency to catch other people's feelings. When someone near you laughs, frowns or sounds anxious, you may start to feel the same way. Elaine Hatfield, John Cacioppo and Richard Rapson described it in detail in the 1990s. They proposed that we automatically mimic other people's faces, voices and postures, and that this mimicry feeds back into our own feelings. Others stress that we also read emotions as information: if everyone around you looks worried, perhaps there is something to worry about. Contagion may help groups coordinate and bond. It may also explain why one bad-tempered colleague can sour a meeting, and why moods seem to spread through families and teams.

study.name: The Facebook news feed experiment
study.who: Adam Kramer, Jamie Guillory and Jeffrey Hancock
study.ref: Kramer, A. D. I., Guillory, J. E., & Hancock, J. T. (2014). Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 111(24), 8788-8790.
study.story: For one week in January 2012, Facebook quietly altered the news feeds of nearly 700,000 English-speaking users. Adam Kramer, a data scientist at the company, worked with Jamie Guillory and Jeffrey Hancock of Cornell University. Some users had a share of their friends' positive posts held back from their feed. Others had a share of negative posts held back. Comparison groups had a similar share of random posts removed. Nothing was deleted, and the hidden posts could still be seen on friends' own pages. The question was whether this would change the emotional tone of what users themselves wrote. A computer program counted the positive and negative words in about three million of their status updates. The results fitted contagion. People who saw fewer positive posts used slightly fewer positive words, and slightly more negative ones. Those who saw fewer negative posts did the reverse. The effects were tiny, a fraction of a percentage point of words, though across a huge network they added up. The bigger reaction, though, was about ethics. Users had not been told they were part of an experiment. The journal published an editorial 'expression of concern', and the study became a landmark in debates about consent and online platforms.
study.finding: Users shown fewer positive posts wrote slightly fewer positive words, and vice versa. The effects went in the predicted direction but were extremely small.

entries.statusNote: Face-to-face contagion is fairly well supported. People mimic expressions and report shifts in mood around others' emotions. Whether mimicry causes those feelings is debated. Large-scale claims are weaker. The Facebook effects were tiny, and word counts are a rough measure of mood. Some studies claimed that happiness or loneliness spreads through social networks over years. Critics noted that similar people tend to befriend each other and share the same surroundings. That can look like contagion. Emotions do spread, but usually modestly.
life: Before a tense conversation, steady yourself first; your mood is likely to spread to the other person.
Notice how much of your mood after scrolling might be borrowed from your feed, and choose what you follow accordingly.
In a team, a leader's visible stress can spread; naming it calmly and steadying yourself helps others too.
entries.myth: Myth: online platforms can easily control our moods on a massive scale. In the famous Facebook study the effect was real but tiny.

quiz.q: What is the most accurate conclusion from the Facebook news feed experiment?
options: Facebook can dramatically change users' moods
The emotional tone of feeds had a real but very small effect on users' posts
Emotions do not spread online at all
Only negative emotions spread
quiz.why: The changes in users' word use went in the expected direction but were extremely small.

entries.title: Stress mindset
entries.line: Seeing stress as potentially helpful, rather than only harmful, may change how people respond to it; early results are promising.
entries.idea: A stress mindset is your belief about what stress does to you. Some people see stress mainly as harmful: it damages health and ruins performance. Others see it as potentially enhancing: it sharpens focus, boosts energy and helps growth. Alia Crum and her colleagues argued that this belief shapes how stress actually affects us. Related work by Jeremy Jamieson asks people to see a racing heart before a test as the body getting ready to perform. The idea is not that stress is good, or that you should seek more of it. It is that the body's stress response evolved to help us meet challenges, and seeing it that way may change how we cope.

study.name: Rethinking stress
study.who: Alia Crum, Peter Salovey and Shawn Achor
study.ref: Crum, A. J., Salovey, P., & Achor, S. (2013). Rethinking stress: The role of mindsets in determining the stress response. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 104(4), 716-733.
study.story: Alia Crum, Peter Salovey and Shawn Achor ran their first study at a large financial company, during a tense period of job cuts and turmoil in banking. They recruited a few hundred employees and randomly assigned them to one of three groups. Over a week, one group watched short videos presenting stress as enhancing. The videos described research suggesting that stress can sharpen focus, deepen relationships and spur growth, with stories of people who rose to the occasion under pressure. A second group watched videos presenting stress as debilitating, stressing its harm to health and work. A third group watched no videos. Before and after, the employees filled in questionnaires about their beliefs, their health and their work. Those who watched the enhancing videos shifted towards a more positive view of stress. They also reported fewer health complaints and better work performance than the other groups. In a second study, students prepared to give a stressful presentation. Those whose mindset saw stress as enhancing showed a more moderate rise and fall in the stress hormone cortisol. They were also keener to receive feedback on their performance. A few minutes of reframing, it seemed, could change how people responded to pressure.
study.finding: Employees shown stress-is-enhancing videos reported fewer health complaints and better work performance than those shown negative videos or none.

entries.statusNote: The early studies were small and relied heavily on self-report. Since then, more work has appeared, including a 2022 paper in Nature by David Yeager and colleagues. It combined stress and growth mindset lessons, and its preregistered experiments (with methods fixed in advance) found benefits for teenagers' stress responses and anxiety. Effects are generally small to moderate and depend on the setting. Reviews call the approach promising, but more independent, large-scale replications are needed before treating it as established.
life: Before an exam or a talk, try telling yourself 'my racing heart is getting me ready' rather than 'I must calm down'.
Treat stress as a sign that something matters to you, then direct the energy into preparing.
Do not use 'stress is good for you' to dismiss someone's chronic overload; a mindset does not fix a bad situation.
entries.myth: Myth: stress is always harmful, so the only goal is to eliminate it. How you view stress seems to matter too, although chronic, severe stress is still bad for health.

quiz.q: What is a stress mindset intervention trying to change?
options: The amount of stress in your life
Your belief about whether stress can be helpful
Your stress hormones directly, with medication
Your workload
quiz.why: It targets beliefs about what stress does to you, not the stressors themselves.

entries.title: Attachment styles
entries.aka: Attachment theory; secure, anxious and avoidant attachment
entries.line: Infants form distinct patterns of attachment to carers, and similar patterns of security and insecurity colour adult relationships.
entries.idea: Attachment theory, begun by the psychiatrist John Bowlby, says babies are built to stay close to a carer who keeps them safe. When that person is reliably available, the child treats them as a secure base: a home port to explore from and return to when frightened. Children whose carers are unpredictable or distant adapt. Some cling and protest (anxious). Others hide their need and act unbothered (avoidant). In adults, researchers now measure two sliding scales rather than fixed boxes: attachment anxiety (worry about being abandoned) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness). Where you sit on these scales colours how you read a late reply, an argument or a partner's need for space. Patterns are fairly stable but can shift with new relationships.

study.name: The Strange Situation
study.who: Mary Ainsworth, Mary Blehar, Everett Waters and Sally Wall
study.ref: Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., & Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of Attachment: A Psychological Study of the Strange Situation. Hillsdale, NJ: Erlbaum.
study.story: In the 1960s and 1970s, Mary Ainsworth wanted a way to see a bond that is normally invisible. She had already spent many hours watching mothers and babies at home, first in Uganda and then in Baltimore. Now she built a short laboratory drama called the Strange Situation. A one-year-old and their mother entered a playroom full of toys. A friendly stranger came in. Then the mother quietly left, came back, left again and returned once more, while observers watched through a one-way window. Ainsworth found that the departures mattered less than the reunions. Most babies cried when their mother left, but greeted her warmly on her return, were soothed quickly and went back to playing. She called them secure. Some babies seemed barely to notice the mother leaving and turned away when she came back, although later studies showed such babies were stressed inside. These she called avoidant. A third group were upset and angry: they sought contact but resisted it, and could not settle. These she called ambivalent or resistant. Later researchers added a fourth, disorganised pattern, in which babies looked confused or frightened. Crucially, Ainsworth linked the lab patterns to what she had seen at home: mothers of secure babies had tended to respond more sensitively to their signals.
study.finding: Most babies in Ainsworth's samples were classed as secure, with smaller groups avoidant or resistant. Secure babies tended to have mothers who had responded more sensitively at home.

entries.statusNote: The Strange Situation is one of the most repeated procedures in developmental psychology. Secure attachment is the most common pattern across many countries, though the mix of insecure types varies by culture. Meta-analyses (studies that pool the results of many studies) find that parental sensitivity is linked to security. But the link is modest, so parenting is not the whole story. Stability from infancy to adulthood is moderate, not fixed. In adults, measures of anxiety and avoidance reliably predict relationship satisfaction. Researchers favour these sliding scales over the neat types sold in pop psychology.
life: If a slow text sends you spiralling, recognise attachment anxiety at work rather than proof of rejection, and ask directly instead of testing your partner.
If you pull away whenever someone gets close, notice it as an old habit of self-protection, and try staying a little longer than feels comfortable.
Be wary of online quizzes that sort you into a fixed type; security can grow through steady, responsive relationships.
entries.myth: Popular culture treats attachment styles as permanent labels stamped in infancy. In fact they are tendencies on sliding scales, shaped by genes, experience and current relationships, and they can change.

quiz.q: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, which moment told researchers most about a baby's attachment?
options: How loudly the baby cried when the mother left
How the baby behaved when the mother came back
How quickly the baby approached the stranger
How many toys the baby played with
quiz.why: Ainsworth found that reunion behaviour, whether the baby sought comfort and settled, best revealed the pattern of attachment.

entries.title: Gottman's four horsemen
entries.line: Criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling during conflict predict unhappy relationships and divorce, with contempt the most corrosive.
entries.idea: John Gottman spent decades filming couples as they argued. He concluded that arguing itself is not the danger; how you argue is. He named four habits the four horsemen. Criticism attacks a partner's character rather than a behaviour ('you never think of anyone but yourself'). Contempt adds scorn: sneering, mockery, eye-rolling, treating the partner as beneath you. Defensiveness deflects blame with excuses or counter-attacks. Stonewalling is shutting down, going silent and withdrawing, often when someone feels flooded by stress. Gottman also suggested antidotes: complain about a specific behaviour, build a habit of appreciation, take some responsibility, and take a break to calm down before trying again. Couples who repair quickly after a harsh moment seem to fare much better.

study.name: The Love Lab newlywed study
study.who: John Gottman, James Coan, Sybil Carrere and Catherine Swanson
study.ref: Gottman, J. M., Coan, J., Carrere, S., & Swanson, C. (1998). Predicting marital happiness and stability from newlywed interactions. Journal of Marriage and the Family, 60(1), 5-22.
study.story: In a university lab in Seattle nicknamed the Love Lab, John Gottman and his colleagues invited about 130 newlywed couples to talk. The researchers asked each couple to pick an ongoing disagreement, perhaps money, in-laws or housework, and discuss it for fifteen minutes while being filmed. Sensors tracked heart rate and other signs of stress. Trained coders then went through the tapes second by second, labelling each facial expression and remark: affection, humour and interest, but also anger, whining, belligerence, defensiveness and contempt. Then the team waited. Over the following six years they checked in with the couples, recording who was still together and how happy they were. Some patterns stood out. Couples who later divorced were more likely to open the discussion harshly and to meet a partner's complaints with contempt or defensiveness. Husbands who refused to accept any influence from their wives were another warning sign. So was a failure to repair: the jokes, apologies and small kind gestures that calm a fight down. Happy, stable couples argued too, sometimes loudly, but they kept a high ratio of positive to negative moments and softened their openings. Gottman's books later turned these findings into the vivid image of four horsemen riding in before the end of a marriage.
study.finding: Couples who later divorced or became unhappy showed more harsh openings, contempt and defensiveness. They also made fewer repair attempts.

entries.statusNote: The idea that hostile, contemptuous conflict harms relationships is well supported by many labs. The famous claim that Gottman can predict divorce with over 90 per cent accuracy is weaker than it sounds. Those figures came from fitting statistical models to the same small samples they described. They did not come from predicting new couples. Critics point out that such models usually do much worse on fresh data. Much of the work also comes from Gottman's own group. The horsemen are a useful, broadly backed warning list, not a precise forecasting tool.
life: Swap 'you always' for a specific complaint: 'I felt hurt when the plans changed without a call.'
Watch for eye-rolling and sarcasm in yourself; contempt seems to do more damage than raised voices.
If your heart is pounding and you cannot listen, call a twenty-minute break and come back, rather than stonewalling.
entries.myth: People often believe a few minutes of video lets experts forecast divorce with near certainty. The accuracy figures came from fitting models to past data; the real lesson is that contempt and stonewalling are bad signs.

quiz.q: According to Gottman's research, what most distinguishes couples who stay happy?
options: They rarely disagree
They argue but avoid contempt and repair quickly
They resolve every issue completely
They keep their conflicts hidden from each other
quiz.why: Stable couples still argued, but they softened their openings, avoided scorn and made frequent repair attempts.

entries.title: Bids for connection
entries.line: Small everyday attempts to get a partner's attention, and whether the partner turns towards them, appear to shape relationship health.
entries.idea: A bid is any small attempt to connect: 'Look at that bird', a sigh, a touch on the arm, a joke, a question about your day. Each bid quietly asks, 'Are you with me?' The other person can turn towards it (respond with interest, even briefly), turn away (miss or ignore it) or turn against it (respond with irritation). John Gottman and his colleagues argue that these tiny moments add up. Turning towards bids builds a store of goodwill and trust that cushions couples during conflict. Turning away, usually from distraction rather than malice, slowly teaches a partner to stop reaching out. The idea applies to friends, colleagues and children as well as romantic partners.

study.name: The apartment lab study
study.ref: Driver, J. L., & Gottman, J. M. (2004). Daily marital interactions and positive affect during marital conflict among newlywed couples. Family Process, 43(3), 301-314.
study.story: To see how couples behave when they are not performing for a camera in a lab, Gottman's team at the University of Washington built something unusual: a small apartment, furnished like a comfortable holiday flat. Newlywed couples were invited to spend a day there. They were asked to live as normally as possible: read the paper, cook, watch television, chat. Cameras on the walls recorded them, and the researchers later combed through hours of footage. Psychologist Janice Driver led much of the coding. She and Gottman were not looking for big dramas. They were looking for tiny moments. A husband glances out of the window and says, 'Wow, look at that boat.' Does his wife look up and say, 'Oh, nice'? Does she keep reading without a word? Or does she snap, 'I'm trying to read'? Coders logged each bid and the response it got. The couples also had a conflict discussion, which was coded for humour and affection. Couples who turned towards each other's everyday bids more often brought more warmth and playfulness into their arguments. In his popular books, Gottman also reports that, years later, couples who were still married had turned towards bids far more often than couples who had divorced.
study.finding: Couples who turned towards each other's small everyday bids showed more humour and affection during conflict. Popular accounts also link turning towards with staying together.

entries.statusNote: The idea is plausible and fits a large body of research showing that everyday responsiveness predicts satisfaction. But the specific bids research rests mostly on small samples from Gottman's own lab. Widely quoted percentages compare couples who stayed together with those who divorced. They come from popular books rather than a detailed peer-reviewed report. They have not been independently replicated (repeated by other researchers). Treat bids as a sensible, partly tested idea, not a precise law.
life: When someone you love says 'Huh, look at this', look up; a three-second response is a small deposit in the relationship.
Notice your own bids that go unanswered, and mention it gently instead of quietly giving up on reaching out.
Put the phone face down at dinner; most missed bids are missed through distraction, not dislike.
entries.myth: Many people think relationships are made or broken in big moments like anniversaries or major rows. The bids idea suggests the ordinary, forgettable exchanges of daily life matter at least as much.

quiz.q: Your partner says 'That's a funny-looking dog' while you are reading. What counts as turning towards this bid?
options: Ignoring it so you can finish your page
Saying 'Not now, I'm busy' sharply
Glancing up and saying 'Ha, it really is'
Changing the subject to something you care about
quiz.why: Turning towards means a brief, interested response that acknowledges the attempt to connect.

entries.title: Responding to good news
entries.line: How a partner responds to your good news, especially with active, enthusiastic interest, predicts closeness and satisfaction in the relationship.
entries.idea: Psychologists call sharing good news capitalisation: you squeeze extra joy out of a happy event by telling someone. Shelly Gable and her colleagues showed that the listener's reaction matters a lot. There are four basic styles. Active-constructive: enthusiastic and curious, asking for details ('That's brilliant! How did they tell you?'). Passive-constructive: warm but low-energy ('Nice, well done'). Active-destructive: pointing out the downsides ('Won't that mean longer hours?'). Passive-destructive: ignoring the news or turning to yourself ('Guess what happened to me today'). Only the first style reliably goes with closer, happier relationships. Surprisingly, in some studies how partners responded to good news predicted relationship quality more strongly than how they responded to bad news.

study.name: What do you do when things go right?
study.who: Shelly Gable, Harry Reis, Emily Impett and Evan Asher
study.ref: Gable, S. L., Reis, H. T., Impett, E. A., & Asher, E. R. (2004). What do you do when things go right? The intrapersonal and interpersonal benefits of sharing positive events. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 87(2), 228-245.
study.story: Shelly Gable, Harry Reis and their colleagues ran a set of studies in the early 2000s around a simple question: what happens when things go right? In one, students kept diaries. Each evening they noted the most positive thing that had happened that day, whether they had told anyone, and how that person had reacted. In another, people in dating and married couples filled in questionnaires describing how their partner usually responded when they shared a success. The researchers sorted the reactions into four kinds by crossing two questions. Was the response active or passive? Was it constructive or destructive? Then they compared these reports with how satisfied, close and committed people felt. The pattern was clear. On days people shared good news, they felt better than the event alone would predict, as if telling it amplified the joy. When the listener responded with active, genuine enthusiasm, people reported higher satisfaction, more intimacy and more trust in the relationship. A lukewarm, polite 'that's nice' did not help, and reactions that found the downside or ignored the news went with worse relationships. A later study by Gable and colleagues brought couples into the lab and filmed them sharing both good and bad events, and found that responses to good news were especially telling.
study.finding: Telling others about positive events boosted wellbeing. Active-constructive responses from partners went with greater satisfaction, intimacy and trust. Passive or deflating responses did not.

entries.statusNote: The link between active-constructive responding and relationship quality has been found repeatedly. It appears across labs, countries and kinds of relationship, including friendships and workplaces. Most of the evidence is correlational: it shows that things go together, not that one causes the other. Happy couples may simply respond more warmly. Experiments that train people to respond actively are fewer, and their effects are smaller. Overall the association is sturdy, and the advice carries little risk.
life: When someone shares good news, ask a follow-up question before saying anything else: 'How did you find out?'
Hold back the 'but' for now; practical worries about the new job can wait until the celebrating is over.
Notice who in your life lights up at your successes; those relationships are worth investing in.
entries.myth: Many people assume support matters most in hard times. Research suggests that how people respond when things go well is at least as important for closeness.

quiz.q: A friend tells you she has been promoted. Which reply is active-constructive?
options: 'Nice.'
'That's amazing! What will you be doing now?'
'Won't that mean a lot more stress?'
'I had a terrible day at work, actually.'
quiz.why: Active-constructive responses are enthusiastic and invite the person to relive and expand on the good news.

entries.title: Perceived partner responsiveness
entries.line: Feeling that a partner understands, values and cares for you is one of the strongest predictors of a good relationship.
entries.idea: Perceived partner responsiveness is the sense that someone gets you. It has three parts: understanding (they grasp what you mean and feel), validation (they respect and accept who you are) and caring (they want good things for you). Harry Reis and Phillip Shaver placed it at the heart of their model of intimacy. You reveal something personal. The other person responds. If you read their response as understanding, valuing and caring, intimacy grows, and you are more willing to share next time. The key word is perceived. What matters most is not what a partner objectively does, but whether you feel understood. That is why the same reply can comfort one person and fall flat for another.

study.name: The intimacy diary study
study.who: Jean-Philippe Laurenceau, Lisa Feldman Barrett and Paula Pietromonaco
study.ref: Laurenceau, J.-P., Feldman Barrett, L., & Pietromonaco, P. R. (1998). Intimacy as an interpersonal process: The importance of self-disclosure, partner disclosure, and perceived partner responsiveness in interpersonal exchanges. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1238-1251.
study.story: In the 1990s Jean-Philippe Laurenceau, Lisa Feldman Barrett and Paula Pietromonaco wanted to test the intimacy model outside the lab, in ordinary life. They recruited university students and asked them to keep a detailed diary of their social interactions for one to two weeks. After every conversation lasting ten minutes or more, participants filled in a short record. How much had they revealed about themselves, both facts and feelings? How much had the other person revealed? How understood, accepted and cared for had they felt? And how intimate did the interaction feel overall? Across many hundreds of recorded conversations with friends, flatmates, partners and family, a consistent picture emerged. Revealing feelings, not just facts, went with greater intimacy. So did the other person's openness. But much of the effect ran through one channel: whether the participant felt the other person had responded with understanding and care. A conversation in which you poured out your heart but felt brushed off was not intimate. A conversation in which you shared a little and felt deeply understood often was. The study gave strong everyday support to the idea that intimacy is a process built from openness and perceived responsiveness together.
study.finding: Revealing yourself, especially your emotions, predicted feelings of intimacy, and so did the partner's openness. Perceived partner responsiveness partly explained these links.

entries.statusNote: Perceived responsiveness is one of the best-supported ideas in relationship science. Many studies link it to satisfaction, commitment and trust. Some long-term studies also link it to better sleep, mood and health, although those links are smaller and less certain.
