Much of the evidence is correlational (showing things go together, not proving cause). But experiments that manipulate responsiveness also change feelings of closeness. In 2020, a large analysis pooled dozens of couple datasets. How people saw their partner, such as the partner's commitment and appreciation, predicted relationship quality better than personal traits.
life: When comforting someone, reflect back what you heard before offering fixes: 'So the worst part was feeling ignored?'
If you feel misunderstood, say what would help ('I just need you to listen'), since responsiveness is judged by the receiver.
Show acceptance of a partner's quirks, not just support in a crisis; feeling valued for who you are builds trust.
entries.myth: People often believe good relationships depend on having lots in common. Feeling understood and cared for predicts satisfaction far better than shared hobbies or matching personalities.

quiz.q: Why does the word 'perceived' matter in perceived partner responsiveness?
options: Because only outside observers can judge responsiveness
Because what counts most is whether you feel understood, not what the partner objectively did
Because responsiveness is an illusion
Because it only applies to new relationships
quiz.why: The benefits flow from feeling understood, valued and cared for, which depends on how a response is received.

entries.title: The 36 questions
entries.line: Strangers who take turns answering increasingly personal questions for 45 minutes feel much closer than strangers who make small talk.
entries.idea: Arthur Aron and his colleagues designed a recipe for closeness in the lab. Two strangers take turns answering 36 questions in three sets, each set more personal than the last. Early questions are gentle ('Would you like to be famous? In what way?'). Later ones go deeper, touching on feelings about family or the last time you cried in front of someone. The final tasks include telling your partner what you like about them. The method works through gradual, mutual self-disclosure: each person reveals a little more, and the other matches it and responds. This builds trust in small, safe steps. The questions were designed to create closeness for research, not love; the love story came later, from the press.

study.name: The experimental generation of closeness
study.who: Arthur Aron, Edward Melinat, Elaine Aron, Robert Vallone and Renee Bator
study.ref: Aron, A., Melinat, E., Aron, E. N., Vallone, R. D., & Bator, R. J. (1997). The experimental generation of interpersonal closeness: A procedure and some preliminary findings. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 23(4), 363-377.
study.story: In the 1990s Arthur Aron, Elaine Aron and their colleagues at the State University of New York at Stony Brook had a practical problem. They wanted to study closeness, but real friendships take months to form. Could they create closeness in under an hour? They paired up students who had never met. Each pair was given the questions on slips of paper. Over 45 minutes they took turns reading them out and answering, spending about fifteen minutes on each set. Some pairs had the escalating personal questions. A comparison group spent the same time on small-talk prompts, such as describing the last concert they had been to or their favourite holiday. Afterwards each student rated how close they felt to their partner, using a simple picture of two circles overlapping by different amounts. The pairs who had answered the personal questions felt markedly closer. The researchers also checked whether it helped to pair people who agreed on important attitudes, or to tell them they would probably like each other; neither made much difference compared with the questions themselves. Nearly two decades later, in 2015, the writer Mandy Len Catron described trying the questions with an acquaintance in a New York Times essay titled 'To Fall in Love With Anyone, Do This'. The questions went viral, and a closeness tool became famous as a love formula.
study.finding: Pairs who worked through the escalating personal questions felt considerably closer. The comparison pairs made small talk for the same length of time.

entries.statusNote: The procedure is one of the most reused tools in social psychology. Its core finding has been replicated (repeated by other researchers) many times, in different countries, online and face to face. It has even been used to build friendships between people of different ethnic groups, reducing anxiety about contact. It reliably boosts feelings of closeness in the short term. What it does not show is that strangers fall in love. There is no good evidence that it creates lasting romance, and long-term effects on friendship are less studied.
life: To deepen a friendship, ask one question a little more personal than usual, and answer it yourself too.
Keep disclosure mutual and gradual; pouring out everything at once can feel like pressure rather than intimacy.
Try a few of the questions on a long car journey or a stale evening in, to break out of routine chat.
entries.myth: The 36 questions are often sold as a way to make anyone fall in love. The study was about closeness between strangers, and it never showed lasting romance.

quiz.q: What makes the 36 questions procedure work?
options: The questions are secretly hypnotic
It produces gradual, mutual and escalating self-disclosure
It forces people to agree on all their views
It only works between people who already fancy each other
quiz.why: Closeness grows as each person reveals a little more and the other matches and responds, step by step.

entries.title: Similarity and attraction
entries.aka: The similarity-attraction effect; birds of a feather
entries.line: People are drawn to others who seem to share their attitudes, but perceived similarity matters more than actual similarity.
entries.idea: In study after study, people like others who agree with them. Similar attitudes, values and backgrounds can feel validating: the other person confirms that your view of the world is right. Similarity also makes conversation easier and suggests that you will get along. But the picture has wrinkles. A large review found that actual similarity, measured objectively, matters most when people barely know each other. In ongoing relationships, what predicts liking is perceived similarity: how alike you believe you are. And we tend to see people we like as more similar to us than they really are. Couples do resemble each other in age, education and values, but they are barely more alike in personality than random pairs.

study.name: The bogus stranger
study.ref: Byrne, D. (1961). Interpersonal attraction and attitude similarity. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 62(3), 713-715.
study.story: Around 1960, Donn Byrne wanted to isolate one ingredient of attraction. Real people differ in looks, voice and charm, which muddies everything. So he invented the bogus stranger. Students first filled in a questionnaire about their attitudes on a wide range of topics, from music and sport to religion, politics and sex before marriage. Some time later they were shown what they were told was the same questionnaire filled in by another student on campus. In fact, the researchers had filled it in themselves. For some students they copied the student's own answers, making the stranger an almost perfect match. For others they wrote the opposite answers. Each student then rated the stranger. Would they like this person? Would they enjoy working with them? How intelligent, moral and well informed did the stranger seem? The results were striking in their simplicity. Students who saw their own views reflected back rated the stranger far more favourably, judging them more likeable, more intelligent and better informed. In many follow-up studies, Byrne found that liking rose steadily with the proportion of attitudes shared, in an almost straight-line relationship. The method became a workhorse of social psychology for decades, because it let researchers turn similarity up or down like a volume knob.
study.finding: Students liked a stranger with matching attitudes far more than one with opposing attitudes. Later work showed liking rose with the proportion of attitudes shared.

entries.statusNote: The bogus stranger effect is robust and has been repeated many times. But a 2008 meta-analysis (a study combining the results of many studies) by Matthew Montoya and colleagues found that actual similarity predicted attraction mostly in brief or imagined encounters. In real, ongoing relationships, perceived similarity mattered much more. Studies of speed-dating and long-term couples find that matching on personality adds little to satisfaction. So similarity does attract, but mainly early on and partly in our heads.
life: On a first meeting, finding shared ground helps; but do not dismiss someone over different tastes in music or films.
Notice that once you like someone, you start to believe you agree with them more than you do.
Salespeople and recruiters often mirror your interests ('I'm a runner too!'); ask whether the similarity is real.
entries.myth: Many believe opposites attract. They mostly do not, but the reverse is overstated too: beyond first impressions, feeling alike matters more than being alike.

quiz.q: What did a large meta-analysis find about similarity in ongoing relationships?
options: Actual similarity in personality strongly predicts happiness
Perceived similarity predicts attraction better than actual similarity
Opposites attract more over time
Similarity has no effect at any stage
quiz.why: In real relationships, believing you are alike mattered more than objectively measured similarity.

entries.title: Proximity and friendship
entries.line: Simple physical nearness strongly predicts who becomes friends, because it creates repeated, easy contact.
entries.idea: Before we can like someone, we have to meet them, and the people we meet most are the ones nearby. That simple fact turns out to be powerful. Neighbours, desk mates and people on the same corridor are far more likely to become friends than people a few doors further away. Proximity works through several routes. It provides chance encounters that cost no effort. Repeated exposure tends to make familiar faces feel safer and more likeable. And people who live or work close together share experiences and expect to keep seeing each other, which encourages getting along. What counts is functional distance, meaning how often paths actually cross, not just distance as the crow flies. The downside is that annoying neighbours can also become intense enemies.

study.name: The Westgate West housing study
study.who: Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back
study.ref: Festinger, L., Schachter, S., & Back, K. (1950). Social Pressures in Informal Groups: A Study of Human Factors in Housing. New York: Harper.
study.story: After the Second World War, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology housed married ex-servicemen studying there in a new development called Westgate West. The flats were in two-storey blocks, with five apartments on each floor. Crucially, families did not choose where to live; they were given whichever unit became free next. To the psychologists Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back, this was a natural experiment. They asked residents a simple question: which three people in the development do you see socially most often? The answers mapped neatly onto the buildings. People were most likely to name their immediate next-door neighbours. Friendship dropped off with every door further along the row. Someone two doors away was a less likely friend than someone next door, even though the difference was only a few metres. Small design details mattered too. Residents of the ground-floor flats at the ends of each block, whose doors were near the stairs used by people living above, made more friends upstairs than other ground-floor residents. People who lived near the postboxes were unusually popular. None of these people had been matched for similarity. The layout of the buildings, and the luck of which door they were given, shaped who they ended up spending time with.
study.finding: Residents were far more likely to befriend next-door neighbours than people a few doors away. Flats on busy routes, such as by the stairs, gained more friends.

entries.statusNote: The link between proximity and friendship has been replicated (found again by other researchers) in student halls, offices and a police academy. At the academy, trainees seated in alphabetical order tended to befriend people with nearby surnames. It remains one of the most reliable findings in social psychology. Modern life complicates it. Online contact lets people bond across great distances, and nearness can intensify dislike as well as liking. But studies of halls and offices still find that small differences in distance shape who connects with whom.
life: If you want new friends, put yourself in repeated, low-effort contact: the same class, the same café, the same corridor.
When choosing a desk or a flat, consider where people naturally pass; it can shape your social life.
Managers can boost collaboration by placing teams that need to talk near shared kitchens or stairs.
entries.myth: People assume friendship is mostly about chemistry and shared interests. Often it starts with something much more ordinary: who happens to live or sit nearby.

quiz.q: In the Westgate West study, why did ground-floor residents near the stairs make more friends?
options: They were the most outgoing people
Upstairs residents passed their doors and met them often
They had larger flats
They were chosen as building leaders
quiz.why: Upstairs residents passed their doors on the way to the stairs, so their paths crossed far more often.

entries.title: The pratfall effect
entries.line: A highly competent person can become more likeable after a small blunder, though the effect depends on who is watching.
entries.idea: We admire competent people, but someone who seems flawless can also feel distant or even threatening. The pratfall effect is the idea that a small, harmless mistake, like spilling coffee, can make an impressive person seem more human and so more likeable. The blunder signals that they are not superhuman, which narrows the gap between them and us. The key condition is that the person must already be seen as highly competent. For someone of ordinary ability, the same slip simply confirms that they are not very good, and it makes them less likeable. Later studies suggested the effect also depends on the observer, including their gender and self-esteem, and that it is not a reliable strategy.

study.name: The spilled coffee study
study.who: Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman and Joanne Floyd
study.ref: Aronson, E., Willerman, B., & Floyd, J. (1966). The effect of a pratfall on increasing interpersonal attractiveness. Psychonomic Science, 4(6), 227-228.
study.story: In 1966 Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman and Joanne Floyd ran an experiment with male students at the University of Minnesota. The students were told they would help judge candidates for a team representing the university in a quiz contest, the kind broadcast on television. Each student listened to a tape recording of an interview with one candidate. In one version the candidate was brilliant. He answered almost every hard question correctly and modestly mentioned his excellent grades, his work on the yearbook and his place on the athletics team. In another version he was mediocre, getting only some questions right and describing an unremarkable record. Then, for half the listeners, something happened at the end of the tape. There was a clatter of crockery, and the candidate exclaimed, 'Oh my goodness, I've spilled coffee all over my new suit.' The other listeners heard no accident. Afterwards the students rated how much they liked the candidate. The brilliant candidate who spilled his coffee was rated the most attractive of all, more likeable than the same brilliant candidate without the accident. The mediocre candidate who spilled coffee was rated the least likeable of the four. A tiny, harmless blunder seemed to help the strong and to hurt the average.
study.finding: Listeners liked the superior candidate most after he spilled coffee. The same blunder made the average candidate the least liked.

entries.statusNote: The original study was small, and used only male students and a single recorded scenario. Direct replications (repeats of the same study) are scarce. Follow-up studies found the effect depended on the listener. It appeared mainly among people of average self-esteem. Work by Kay Deaux suggested it was weaker or absent among women. More recent research on admitting mistakes and showing vulnerability finds benefits in some settings but not others. The idea that perfection can feel off-putting has some support, but the pratfall effect itself is fragile and situational.
life: If you are already seen as very capable, admitting a small mistake openly may make you more approachable, not less.
Do not stage clumsiness to win people over; for anyone not already seen as competent, a blunder simply looks like a blunder.
Notice when a polished speaker's humble slip may be a rehearsed technique to win your trust.
entries.myth: The pratfall effect is often retold as 'mistakes make you likeable'. In the original study, a blunder only helped someone already seen as excellent, and it hurt the average candidate.

quiz.q: In Aronson's study, who became more likeable after spilling coffee?
options: Everyone who spilled coffee
Only the average candidate
Only the highly competent candidate
Nobody; the blunder always hurt
quiz.why: The blunder humanised the impressive candidate but made the average candidate seem less likeable.

entries.title: Self-expansion
entries.aka: The self-expansion model; shared novel activities
entries.line: People are drawn to relationships that broaden who they are, and sharing new, exciting activities may rekindle a couple's closeness.
entries.idea: Arthur and Elaine Aron's self-expansion model says humans have a basic drive to grow: to gain new skills, perspectives and experiences. A close relationship is one of the main ways we do this. Early in love, we expand fast, absorbing a partner's friends, music, ideas and ways of seeing the world. That rapid growth feels thrilling. Over time the pace slows and the relationship can feel stale, not because anything is wrong but because there is less that is new to absorb. The model suggests a fix: do new and challenging things together. Shared novelty brings back some of the excitement of early growth, and couples may link that good feeling with each other.

study.name: The Velcro task
study.who: Arthur Aron, Christina Norman, Elaine Aron, Colin McKenna and Richard Heyman
study.ref: Aron, A., Norman, C. C., Aron, E. N., McKenna, C., & Heyman, R. E. (2000). Couples' shared participation in novel and arousing activities and experienced relationship quality. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 273-284.
study.story: In the late 1990s Arthur Aron and his colleagues brought married couples into a lab and gave some of them a ridiculous task. Gym mats were laid out on the floor with a soft barrier in the middle. The partners were strapped together with Velcro at one wrist and one ankle, as in a three-legged race. They then had to move along the mats, climb over the barrier and come back, while holding a pillow between their bodies without using their hands. They were timed, and told they could win a prize if they beat the clock. Unsurprisingly, there was a lot of stumbling and laughter. Other couples were given a dull task instead: one partner slowly rolled a ball to the middle of the mat while the other watched, and then they swapped. Before and after the activities, the couples answered questions about how satisfied they were with their relationship, and in some studies they were filmed discussing a topic so that observers could rate their warmth. The couples who had struggled through the silly, novel and physically demanding task reported higher relationship quality afterwards than those who had done the boring one. The researchers also found that couples who said they did more exciting things together in everyday life tended to be more satisfied.
study.finding: Couples who did the novel, challenging task together reported bigger gains in satisfaction than couples given a mundane task.

entries.statusNote: The self-expansion model has wide support from surveys, diary studies and experiments. It helps explain why new relationships feel exhilarating. The specific claim that a novel activity boosts satisfaction rests on fairly small studies. The effects are modest and may be short-lived. In an early field study, couples assigned exciting dates for ten weeks gained more satisfaction than couples assigned pleasant ones. But such studies are few, and large preregistered replications (repeats with the plan registered in advance) are lacking. The broad idea is well supported; the quick fix is less certain.
life: Swap the usual restaurant for something neither of you has tried: a dance class, a walk somewhere new, a cooking challenge.
Notice that boredom in a long relationship may signal a lack of growth, not a lack of love.
In friendships too, learning something side by side keeps the bond fresh.
entries.myth: People often assume that when a relationship feels flat, the spark is gone for good. The model suggests shared novelty can bring back some of that early excitement.

quiz.q: According to the self-expansion model, why do long relationships often feel less exciting?
options: Partners grow to dislike each other
There is less that is new to learn and absorb from each other
Love hormones run out after exactly two years
People become more selfish over time
quiz.why: The thrill of early love comes partly from rapid growth, which naturally slows as partners get to know each other.

entries.title: The shaky bridge study
entries.aka: Misattribution of arousal; the Capilano bridge experiment
entries.line: People sometimes mistake the racing heart of fear or exercise for attraction to someone nearby.
entries.idea: Physical arousal (a pounding heart, quick breathing, sweaty palms) feels much the same whatever causes it. The misattribution idea, which builds on Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory of emotion, says we look around to explain such feelings and can pin them on the wrong cause. If you meet someone attractive while your body is already stirred up by fear, exercise or excitement, you may partly read that arousal as attraction to them. This works best when the true cause is not obvious. If you know your heart is racing because you have just run for the bus, you discount it. The idea may help explain why thrilling dates, scary films and shared adventures are sometimes linked with romance.

study.name: The Capilano Suspension Bridge study
study.ref: Dutton, D. G., & Aron, A. P. (1974). Some evidence for heightened sexual attraction under conditions of high anxiety. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 30(4), 510-517.
study.story: In the early 1970s Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron set up an experiment on two bridges near Vancouver in British Columbia, Canada. The first was the Capilano Suspension Bridge, a narrow walkway of wooden boards hung from wire cables, which sways and wobbles about 70 metres above rocks and rapids. The second was a sturdy wooden bridge further upstream, only a few metres above a gentle stream. Men crossing either bridge alone were approached by an attractive young woman. She explained that she was doing a project for her psychology class and asked them to fill in a short questionnaire, which included writing a brief story about an ambiguous picture of a woman. Afterwards she tore off a corner of the page, wrote down her name and phone number, and said they could call her if they wanted to hear more about the study. The researchers then looked at two things. First, the stories written on the frightening bridge contained more sexual imagery. Second, far more of the men from the frightening bridge actually phoned the woman: about half, compared with only a few from the safe bridge. When the interviewer was a man, the difference between the bridges largely disappeared. Dutton and Aron argued that the men had mislabelled their fear as attraction.
study.finding: Men interviewed on the frightening bridge wrote more sexual stories. They were also much more likely to phone the female interviewer than men on the safe bridge.

entries.statusNote: In 1998, Craig Foster and colleagues ran a meta-analysis (a study combining many studies). Arousal from unrelated sources did tend to increase attraction. But this may work through automatic processes rather than conscious mislabelling. The original bridge study was small, with only a few dozen men. Men who chose to cross a scary bridge may have differed from those who did not. Large preregistered replications (repeats with the plan registered in advance) are scarce. So the effect is probably smaller and less reliable than its fame suggests.
life: A thrilling first date, such as a rollercoaster or a scary film, might boost the spark, but do not mistake adrenaline for long-term compatibility.
Before deciding you have fallen for someone on holiday or at a festival, ask how much of the feeling comes from the setting.
Notice when loud music, crowds or a sense of urgency make a product or a person feel more appealing than they are.
entries.myth: The study is often retold as proof that danger reliably makes people fall in love. The effect is modest, depends on not noticing the true cause of the arousal, and rests on small original samples.

quiz.q: When would misattribution of arousal be least likely to happen?
options: When the cause of the racing heart is obvious
When the other person is attractive
When the setting is exciting
When the person is unsure why they feel stirred up
quiz.why: People discount arousal they can clearly explain, so misattribution needs the real cause to be unclear.

entries.title: The Big Five
entries.line: Much of human personality can be described by five broad traits that are measurable, fairly stable and predictive of life outcomes.
entries.idea: The Big Five are five broad dimensions of personality: openness to experience (curiosity, imagination), conscientiousness (organisation, self-discipline), extraversion (sociability, energy), agreeableness (warmth, cooperation) and neuroticism (a tendency to feel anxious or low). They grew out of the idea that important differences between people get captured in everyday language. When researchers analysed thousands of descriptive words and questionnaire answers, five clusters kept appearing. Each trait is a sliding scale, not a type, and most people sit near the middle. Traits are partly inherited and fairly stable in adulthood, but they shift gradually with age: on average, people become more conscientious and agreeable, and less neurotic, as they mature.

study.name: Five factors across instruments and observers
study.ref: McCrae, R. R., & Costa, P. T. (1987). Validation of the five-factor model of personality across instruments and observers. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 52(1), 81-90.
study.story: By the 1980s many psychologists suspected that five broad traits could summarise personality, but critics had a fair objection. Perhaps the five factors were just a quirk of particular questionnaires, or of the flattering way people like to see themselves. Robert McCrae and Paul Costa, working at the US National Institute on Aging, set out to test this. They drew on volunteers from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, a long-running project that followed hundreds of adults over many years. Participants rated themselves on different kinds of personality measure, including long lists of opposite adjectives, such as careless versus careful, and full questionnaires. Then the researchers went further. They asked people who knew each participant well, such as friends, neighbours and spouses, to rate that person too, independently. If the five factors were only a product of self-flattery, the outsiders' ratings should not line up. In fact they did. The same five dimensions emerged from adjective ratings and from questionnaires, and from self-reports and peer ratings alike. A participant who described himself as anxious and disorganised tended to be described that way by his spouse and friends too. The agreement was far from perfect, but it was substantial across all five traits.
study.finding: The same five factors appeared across different measures, and in both self and peer ratings. Observers agreed substantially with people's descriptions of themselves.

entries.statusNote: The Big Five is the leading model in personality research. It holds up well across many countries and languages, though some non-Western samples show messier patterns. A six-factor model called HEXACO, which adds honesty-humility, is a serious rival. Traits predict real outcomes such as health, job performance and relationship stability. In 2019, Christopher Soto tried to replicate (repeat with new samples) 78 published links between traits and life outcomes. Most replicated, though usually with somewhat smaller effects. The effects are real but modest for any one person.
life: Prefer Big Five tests to type tests like the Myers-Briggs; they are better supported and treat traits as scales, not boxes.
If you score low on conscientiousness, lean on systems such as calendars, reminders and routines rather than willpower alone.
Remember that traits shift with age and circumstance; your personality at twenty is not your fixed fate.
entries.myth: Many people think personality tests sort you into a type. The evidence supports traits as continuous scales, and popular type systems such as the Myers-Briggs have much weaker scientific backing.

quiz.q: Why did McCrae and Costa collect ratings from friends and spouses?
options: To check the five traits were not just self-flattery or a quirk of one questionnaire
To diagnose mental illness
To find each person's true personality type
To measure intelligence
quiz.why: Agreement between self and peer ratings showed the five factors reflected real, observable differences between people.

entries.title: The spotlight effect
entries.aka: Egocentric bias in judging how noticeable we are
entries.line: People overestimate how much others notice their appearance and actions, whether embarrassing or impressive.
entries.idea: When you trip on a step, have a bad hair day or say something awkward, it can feel as if everyone saw. The spotlight effect is our tendency to overestimate how much other people notice and remember about us. It happens because we are the centre of our own experience. We know every detail of what we did and how we felt, and we struggle to adjust enough for the fact that others are busy with their own concerns, including their own spotlights. The effect applies to good things too: people overestimate how much others notice their clever remark or new haircut. A related bias, the illusion of transparency, is the belief that our inner nerves are more visible to others than they really are.

study.name: The Barry Manilow T-shirt
study.who: Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky
study.ref: Gilovich, T., Medvec, V. H., & Savitsky, K. (2000). The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211-222.
study.story: In the late 1990s Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky at Cornell University devised a deliberately embarrassing test. Students arrived one at a time for what they thought was an ordinary study, and were asked to put on a T-shirt bearing a large picture of Barry Manilow, a singer whom students at the time considered deeply uncool. Each wearer was then led into a room where a group of other students were already seated, filling in questionnaires. After a brief moment, the experimenter took the wearer back out again. Outside, the wearer was asked to estimate how many of the people in the room could say who was on the shirt. Wearers guessed that roughly half of the observers had noticed. The researchers then asked the observers. Only about a quarter could name the face on the shirt. The wearers had roughly doubled the attention they were getting. The team repeated the idea with shirts showing figures students admired, such as Bob Marley or Martin Luther King Jr., and found a similar but smaller overestimate. In further studies, people in group discussions overestimated how much others had noticed both their contributions and their slip-ups. Being at the centre of your own world makes it easy to forget that you are not at the centre of everyone else's.
study.finding: T-shirt wearers guessed that about half the observers had noticed the embarrassing shirt. In fact only about a quarter had.

entries.statusNote: The spotlight effect has been reproduced in many variations, from embarrassing clothing to sports performance and conversations. It fits a wider body of research on egocentric thinking. The original studies were modest in size. Large preregistered replications (repeats with the plan registered in advance) are fewer than for some other effects. Even so, the basic pattern seems sturdy. The size of the overestimate varies with the situation. But the direction keeps turning up: we feel more noticed than we are.
life: After an awkward moment, remind yourself that most people were thinking about themselves, not about you.
If nerves stop you speaking up, remember that others notice your small stumbles far less than you do.
It applies to wins too: do not expect everyone to notice your new haircut or clever comment; tell people what you want them to know.
entries.myth: People assume everyone noticed their blunder and will remember it. In reality most observers barely registered it and soon forget.

quiz.q: Why does the spotlight effect happen?
options: Other people are secretly very observant
We start from our own vivid experience and fail to adjust for how distracted others are
We secretly want to be noticed
It only happens to shy people
quiz.why: We anchor on our own detailed view of ourselves and do not adjust enough for how little attention others pay.

entries.title: Self-serving bias
entries.line: People tend to credit their successes to themselves and to blame their failures on circumstances or bad luck.
entries.idea: When things go well, we tend to think 'I worked hard' or 'I'm good at this'. When they go badly, we think 'the test was unfair' or 'I was unlucky'. This lopsided pattern of explanation is the self-serving bias. It protects self-esteem and keeps us motivated, which may be why it is so widespread. It shows up in exams, sport, work and relationships. The bias is not equal everywhere. It tends to be weaker in some East Asian cultures, which place more value on self-criticism and modesty. It is also weaker in people with depression, who often judge themselves more harshly, though whether more accurately is debated. A mild version may be part of normal, healthy functioning.

study.name: A meta-analysis of self-serving attributions
study.who: Amy Mezulis, Lyn Abramson, Janet Hyde and Benjamin Hankin
study.ref: Mezulis, A. H., Abramson, L. Y., Hyde, J. S., & Hankin, B. L. (2004). Is there a universal positivity bias in attributions? A meta-analytic review of individual, developmental, and cultural differences in the self-serving attributional bias. Psychological Bulletin, 130(5), 711-747.
study.story: How strong is the self-serving bias, and is it the same for everyone? In 2004 Amy Mezulis, Lyn Abramson, Janet Hyde and Benjamin Hankin set out to answer this by pulling together decades of research. Most of the studies they gathered followed a similar script. People did a task, such as solving puzzles, taking a test or playing a game. They were then told they had done well or badly, often regardless of how they had really performed. Finally they were asked why. Was it their ability and effort, or the difficulty of the task and luck? The team combined the results of hundreds of such studies, involving tens of thousands of participants of many ages and from many countries. This kind of analysis is called a meta-analysis: a study of studies, which weighs all the evidence together rather than relying on any single experiment. The verdict was clear. Across the whole body of research, people showed a large and consistent tendency to take credit for success and to avoid blame for failure. But its size varied in revealing ways. The bias was largest in children and in older adults, and smaller in middle age. It was smaller in Asian samples than in American and European ones. And it was much weaker among people with depression, anxiety or other psychological problems.
study.finding: Across hundreds of studies the self-serving bias was large and consistent. But it was smaller in Asian samples and in middle age. It was much weaker among people with psychological problems.

entries.statusNote: The self-serving bias is one of the most robust findings about how people explain events. This large meta-analysis and many later studies confirm it. Debates continue about why it happens. It may protect self-esteem or manage how others see us. Or we may simply expect success, so failure feels surprising and seems to need an outside cause. Cultural differences are real but sometimes overstated; the bias appears in most groups studied. The basic pattern holds up well.
life: After a failure, ask what you could have done differently, even if luck played a part; that is where the learning is.
In arguments about chores, remember that both of you probably credit yourselves with more than your fair share.
Be sceptical when leaders credit wins to their strategy but blame losses on market conditions.
entries.myth: Many people think only arrogant people show this bias. In fact it is close to universal and mostly unconscious, and a mild version may even support mental health.

quiz.q: Which group showed a much weaker self-serving bias in the meta-analysis?
options: Children
Older adults
People with depression
American students
quiz.why: People with depression tended not to protect themselves this way, explaining success and failure more evenly.

entries.title: The placebo effect
entries.aka: Placebo response; expectation effects in treatment
entries.line: Treatments with no active ingredient can ease symptoms like pain and nausea, partly through expectation and the experience of care.
entries.idea: A placebo is a dummy treatment, such as a sugar pill or a fake procedure, with no active ingredient. Yet people given placebos often feel better. Some of this is not the placebo at all. Illnesses naturally rise and fall, and people tend to seek help at their worst and then improve anyway, a pattern called regression to the mean. Patients may also report what they think doctors want to hear. But part of the effect is real. Expecting relief can trigger the brain's own pain-relieving chemicals and change how symptoms are felt. The ritual of treatment, a caring clinician, even the colour and price of a pill, all shape expectations. Placebo effects are strongest for subjective symptoms such as pain, nausea and fatigue.

study.name: Placebos without deception
study.ref: Kaptchuk, T. J., Friedlander, E., Kelley, J. M., Sanchez, M. N., Kokkotou, E., Singer, J. P., Kowalczykowski, M., Miller, F. G., Kirsch, I., & Lembo, A. J. (2010). Placebos without deception: A randomized controlled trial in irritable bowel syndrome. PLoS ONE, 5(12), e15591.
study.story: Could a placebo work even if patients knew it was a placebo? In 2010 Ted Kaptchuk and his colleagues at Harvard tested this with people suffering from irritable bowel syndrome, a painful gut condition with no simple cure. They recruited around eighty patients and split them at random into two groups. One group received no treatment. The other was handed a bottle clearly labelled 'placebo pills' and told the truth: these were inert pills, like sugar pills, containing no medicine. But the doctors also explained, warmly and in detail, that placebos had produced real improvement in earlier studies through mind and body processes, and that patients did not need to believe in them, only to take them faithfully twice a day. Many patients were sceptical, even amused. Both groups had the same amount of friendly contact with the staff. Over three weeks, everyone kept track of their symptoms. At the end, the open placebo group reported significantly greater improvement in symptoms and quality of life than the untreated group, where significantly means the difference was unlikely to be due to chance. The study was small and short, and everyone knew which group they were in, but it challenged the assumption that placebos only work through deception. Later trials have tested open-label placebos for back pain and other conditions.
study.finding: Patients given openly labelled placebo pills reported significantly more symptom relief than untreated patients. They knew all along that the pills were inert.

entries.statusNote: Placebo effects are real but often oversold. A famous 1950s claim that placebos help about a third of patients ignored natural recovery. In 2001, Asbjørn Hróbjartsson and Peter Gøtzsche compared placebo with no treatment across many trials. They found little effect on objective outcomes, such as blood tests. But there were small benefits for pain and other self-reported symptoms. Brain research confirms that expectation can trigger natural pain relief. Open-label placebo trials are promising, but most are small and patients know their group, so larger tests are needed.
life: Expecting your treatment to help, and trusting your clinician, can genuinely improve how you feel.
When a remedy seemed to work, ask whether you would have got better anyway; many illnesses improve on their own.
Be wary of pricey wellness products whose only proof is that users feel better; placebos can do that too.
entries.myth: Many people think placebos can cure almost anything if you believe hard enough. They mainly change how symptoms like pain feel, not tumours, infections or blood test results.

quiz.q: Why does much of the improvement seen in placebo groups not come from the placebo itself?
options: Placebo pills contain hidden drugs
Many conditions improve naturally, and people often seek treatment at their worst
Doctors fake the results
People only improve when they are deceived
quiz.why: Natural recovery and regression to the mean explain much of the change, so trials need a no-treatment group to measure the true placebo effect.

entries.title: The Pygmalion effect
entries.aka: Teacher expectancy effect; the Rosenthal effect
entries.line: What teachers and leaders expect of people can shape their performance, though the effects are usually small.
entries.idea: The Pygmalion effect is a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy: a belief about someone that helps make itself come true. If a teacher expects a pupil to do well, the teacher may give that child warmer attention, harder work, more time to answer and more helpful feedback. The pupil responds to this treatment and does better, apparently confirming the expectation. Low expectations can work the other way, which is sometimes called the golem effect. The name comes from the myth of Pygmalion, a sculptor whose statue came to life, and from George Bernard Shaw's play in which a professor transforms a flower seller. Similar effects have been studied in workplaces, the military and sport.

study.name: Pygmalion in the Classroom
study.ref: Rosenthal, R., & Jacobson, L. (1968). Pygmalion in the Classroom: Teacher Expectation and Pupils' Intellectual Development. New York: Holt, Rinehart and Winston.
study.story: In the mid-1960s the psychologist Robert Rosenthal and the head teacher Lenore Jacobson carried out an experiment in a primary school in California, which they called Oak School. At the start of the year every child took what teachers were told was a new test that could spot pupils about to bloom intellectually. They gave it an impressive name: the Harvard Test of Inflected Acquisition. It was really a standard nonverbal intelligence test. Rosenthal and Jacobson then chose about one child in five completely at random and told the teachers that these pupils were likely to show unusual gains in the coming year. Nothing else changed: the children were not told, and they received no special programme. At the end of the year all the pupils took the test again. Overall, the supposed bloomers gained a few more IQ points than their classmates. The difference was concentrated in the youngest classes. In the first and second grades, the labelled children made much bigger gains than the others; in older years the difference was small or absent. The researchers concluded that teachers' raised expectations had somehow been communicated to the children and helped them improve. Published in 1968 as a book, the study made headlines and shaped debates about education and inequality.
study.finding: Children randomly labelled as bloomers gained more IQ points than their classmates. The effect appeared mainly in the first two grades.

entries.statusNote: The original study was heavily criticised. The test worked poorly for the youngest children, some scores were implausible, and the overall effect rested on a few classes. Many attempts to replicate it (repeat it in other schools) gave weak or no effects. In 1984, Stephen Raudenbush ran a meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies). The effect appeared mainly when teachers had known pupils only briefly. Later reviews by Lee Jussim and Kent Harber concluded that teacher expectations do affect achievement. But the effects are small, tend to fade, and may be larger for disadvantaged groups.
life: As a parent or manager, show genuine belief in someone's growth through challenge and useful feedback, not just praise.
Notice who you give the hard questions and the extra time to; expectations often leak out in small behaviours.
Remember that expectations work at the margins; they help, but they do not transform ability on their own.
entries.myth: The story is often told as proof that believing in a child can raise their IQ dramatically. The real effects are modest, often short-lived and strongest when teachers know little else about the pupil.

quiz.q: According to Raudenbush's meta-analysis, when did fake labels about pupils matter most?
options: When teachers had known the pupils for years
When teachers had known the pupils only briefly
When the pupils were told about the label
In secondary schools
quiz.why: Fake labels had most influence when teachers had little real information about the pupils yet.

entries.title: The Barnum effect
entries.line: People rate vague, general personality descriptions as remarkably accurate accounts of themselves.
entries.idea: The Barnum effect is our tendency to accept vague, flattering statements as precise descriptions of our own personality. Statements like 'You have a great need for other people to like you' or 'At times you are outgoing, but at other times you are reserved' apply to almost everyone. Yet when they are presented as a personal reading, they feel uncannily accurate. The effect is named after the showman P. T. Barnum, whose shows were said to have something for everybody. It explains much of the appeal of horoscopes, palm reading, many online personality quizzes and psychic readings. The effect is stronger when people believe the description was made just for them, when it is mostly positive, and when it comes from an apparent authority.

study.name: The fallacy of personal validation
study.ref: Forer, B. R. (1949). The fallacy of personal validation: A classroom demonstration of gullibility. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 44(1), 118-123.
study.story: In 1948 the psychologist Bertram Forer gave his introductory psychology students a personality test he called the Diagnostic Interest Blank. A week later he handed each student what appeared to be a personal analysis based on their answers, with their name on it. He asked them to rate how well it described them, on a scale from zero (poor) to five (perfect), and to say how well they thought the test worked. The students were impressed. Most gave their profile a four or a five, and the average rating was above four. Many felt the test had captured them with startling insight. Then Forer revealed the trick. Every student had received exactly the same profile. It was made of thirteen statements, many of them taken from a newsstand astrology book. They included lines such as 'You have a great deal of unused capacity which you have not turned to your advantage', 'Disciplined and self-controlled outside, you tend to be worrisome and insecure inside' and 'Security is one of your major goals in life'. The general, double-edged statements fitted nearly everyone. Forer published his classroom demonstration in 1949 under a pointed title, warning fellow psychologists that a client's agreement with a reading proves very little about whether the reading is accurate.
study.finding: Students rated an identical, generic profile as an accurate description of their own personality. The average score was above four out of five.

entries.statusNote: The Barnum effect is one of the most reliably reproduced demonstrations in psychology. Many replications (repeats of the study) since the 1950s show the same pattern. Dickson and Kelly reviewed them in the 1980s, covering horoscopes, handwriting analysis and computer-generated profiles. Its strength varies: it is larger for positive statements and when people believe the reading is personal to them. It does not mean all personality tests are useless. But a test feeling accurate is poor evidence that it is.
life: When a horoscope or quiz feels spot on, check whether the same words would fit your friends equally well.
Judge personality tests by research on what they predict, not by how accurate your result feels.
Watch for cold reading by psychics and some salespeople: broad, flattering guesses that you fill in yourself.
entries.myth: People think a reading that feels accurate must be accurate. The Barnum effect shows that almost any vague, flattering profile feels accurate to almost anyone.

quiz.q: Why did Forer's students rate the profile as so accurate?
options: The test genuinely measured their personalities
The statements were vague and true of nearly everyone
Forer wrote each profile individually
They were trying to please their teacher
quiz.why: General, double-edged statements fit almost anyone, but feel personal when presented as an individual reading.

entries.title: Self-compassion
entries.line: Treating yourself with the kindness you would show a friend after a setback goes with better wellbeing than harsh self-criticism.
entries.idea: The psychologist Kristin Neff defines self-compassion as three things working together. Self-kindness means responding to your own failures with warmth rather than attack. Common humanity means remembering that everyone struggles and makes mistakes, so you are not uniquely flawed. Mindfulness means noticing painful feelings without ignoring them or being swept away by them. Self-compassion differs from self-esteem, which depends on judging yourself as good, or better than others, and can collapse after failure. Many people fear that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. Research suggests the opposite: people who are self-compassionate after a mistake are often more willing to admit it and try to improve, because failure feels less threatening.

study.name: The doughnut study
study.ref: Adams, C. E., & Leary, M. R. (2007). Promoting self-compassionate attitudes toward eating among restrictive and guilty eaters. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 26(10), 1120-1144.
study.story: In a 2007 study, Claire Adams and Mark Leary at Wake Forest University in North Carolina investigated a familiar problem: why breaking a diet so often leads to eating even more. They invited young women to the lab for what was described as a study of food tasting. Most of the women first ate a doughnut and drank a glass of water, a small diet-breaking moment for anyone trying to restrict their eating. Then some of them received a short, kind message from the experimenter. She mentioned that people often feel bad about eating unhealthy food in studies like this, but that everyone eats like this sometimes, and that there was no reason to be really hard on themselves. The others got no such message. Next came a supposed taste test. Each woman was left alone with bowls of sweets and told to eat as much as she liked while rating the flavours. Afterwards, the researchers secretly weighed how much had been eaten. Among women who usually restricted their eating or felt guilty about food, the results differed sharply. Those who had heard no kind message tended to eat more sweets after the doughnut, as if thinking that the diet was ruined anyway. Those who had received the self-compassionate message ate less and reported feeling less distressed.
study.finding: Restrictive and guilty eaters who heard a brief self-compassionate message ate fewer sweets after the doughnut. They also felt less distressed than those who heard no message.

entries.statusNote: Self-compassion is consistently linked with lower depression and anxiety and higher wellbeing. Meta-analyses (studies pooling many studies) find these associations are large. A 2019 meta-analysis of self-compassion programmes by Madeleine Ferrari and colleagues found moderate benefits. But much evidence is correlational (showing things go together, not cause). Many trials are small or compare against no treatment. Critics also argue the main questionnaire partly measures low neuroticism, a calm, unworried temperament. Single-session lab effects, like the doughnut study, have rarely been tested in large replications. Promising, but less settled than it looks.
life: After a mistake, ask what you would say to a friend in the same spot, then say that to yourself.
If you slip on a goal, treat it as a blip rather than a reason to give up entirely.
Remind yourself that struggling is part of being human, not proof that you alone are failing.
entries.myth: Many people think self-compassion is self-indulgence that kills motivation. Studies suggest it often makes people more willing to own their mistakes and keep trying.

quiz.q: How does self-compassion differ from self-esteem?
options: It means rating yourself above others
It offers kindness whether you succeed or fail, rather than depending on judging yourself as good
It is exactly the same thing
It means ignoring your mistakes
quiz.why: Self-esteem rests on judging yourself favourably, while self-compassion stays available after failure.

entries.title: Cognitive distortions and CBT
entries.line: Habitual, distorted ways of thinking feed depression and anxiety, and learning to spot and test them is the core of CBT.
entries.idea: In the 1960s the psychiatrist Aaron Beck noticed that his depressed patients shared characteristic patterns of thought. They saw themselves, the world and the future in a bleak, biased way. He called these automatic thoughts and identified common distortions: all-or-nothing thinking ('I failed once, so I'm a failure'), catastrophising (assuming the worst), mind reading (assuming others think badly of you), overgeneralising and discounting the positive. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) teaches people to notice these thoughts, examine the evidence for and against them, and test them through small behavioural experiments, such as going to the party and seeing what actually happens. The aim is not positive thinking but more accurate thinking, which in turn changes feelings and behaviour.

study.name: Cognitive therapy versus antidepressants
study.who: John Rush, Aaron Beck, Maria Kovacs and Steven Hollon
study.ref: Rush, A. J., Beck, A. T., Kovacs, M., & Hollon, S. (1977). Comparative efficacy of cognitive therapy and pharmacotherapy in the treatment of depressed outpatients. Cognitive Therapy and Research, 1(1), 17-37.
study.story: In the 1970s the standard treatment for depression was medication, and talking therapy was widely seen as a slower, weaker option. John Rush, Aaron Beck, Maria Kovacs and Steven Hollon at the University of Pennsylvania decided to put Beck's new cognitive therapy to a direct test. They recruited a few dozen adults with moderate to severe depression from outpatient clinics. About half were randomly assigned to cognitive therapy, with up to twenty sessions over twelve weeks. In these sessions patients learned to track their mood and thoughts, catch moments of all-or-nothing or catastrophic thinking, weigh the evidence, and plan activities that tested their gloomy predictions. The others received imipramine, a widely used antidepressant, with regular check-ins with a psychiatrist. Random assignment meant that, on average, the two groups started out alike, so differences at the end could be put down to the treatment. By the end of treatment both groups had improved, but those given cognitive therapy had improved more, on both their own ratings and clinicians' ratings of depression. Fewer of them dropped out. A follow-up suggested the gains tended to last. For a psychological therapy to match, let alone beat, a standard drug was startling at the time, and the study helped launch CBT as a mainstream treatment.
study.finding: Depressed outpatients given cognitive therapy improved more than those given the antidepressant imipramine. They also dropped out less often over the twelve weeks.

entries.statusNote: CBT is among the most tested therapies. Hundreds of randomised trials (in which patients are assigned to treatments by chance) show it helps depression, anxiety disorders and more. But the early study's clear win over medication has not held up. Later, larger trials found CBT and antidepressants broadly comparable, with CBT perhaps better at preventing relapse. Meta-analyses (studies pooling many trials) by Pim Cuijpers and colleagues show smaller effects in high-quality trials. CBT is also not clearly better than other well-run therapies. Whether changing distorted thoughts is the main reason it works is still debated.
life: When you notice a sudden drop in mood, write down the thought behind it and ask what the evidence is for and against it.
Watch for 'always', 'never' and 'everyone' in your self-talk; they often signal all-or-nothing thinking.
Test a fearful prediction with a small experiment, then compare what happened with what you expected.
entries.myth: CBT is often caricatured as forced positive thinking. It aims at balanced, evidence-based thinking, and it works on behaviour as well as thoughts.

quiz.q: What does CBT mainly ask people to do with a gloomy automatic thought?
options: Replace it with a cheerful affirmation
Suppress it completely
Examine the evidence and test it against reality
Accept it as a deep truth
quiz.why: CBT treats thoughts as guesses to be tested, aiming for accuracy rather than forced positivity.

entries.title: Gratitude practices
entries.line: Regularly noting things you are grateful for can modestly lift mood and life satisfaction, though effects are smaller than often claimed.
entries.idea: Gratitude practices ask people to pay deliberate attention to the good things in their lives. Common versions include writing a weekly list of things you are thankful for, keeping a 'three good things' diary each evening, or writing and delivering a letter of thanks to someone who helped you. The idea is that our minds drift towards problems and quickly get used to good fortune. Deliberately noticing the good may counter that drift, boost positive emotions and strengthen relationships, since gratitude often turns attention towards other people. The practices are cheap and quick, which makes them popular in schools, workplaces and self-help books. The real question is how much they change, and for whom.

study.name: Counting blessings versus burdens
study.ref: Emmons, R. A., & McCullough, M. E. (2003). Counting blessings versus burdens: An experimental investigation of gratitude and subjective well-being in daily life. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 84(2), 377-389.
study.story: Around the turn of the millennium, Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough ran one of the first experiments on gratitude, with university students taking a health psychology course. The students were randomly split into groups and asked to keep a weekly journal for ten weeks. Once a week, one group wrote down up to five things in their lives they were grateful for. Students listed things like waking up in the morning, the generosity of friends and, in one case, the Rolling Stones. A second group wrote down up to five hassles, such as hard-to-find parking, a messy kitchen or money problems. A third group simply listed five events that had affected them, good or bad. Each week everyone also rated their mood, their physical symptoms such as headaches, how they felt about their life as a whole, and how much they had exercised. At the end of the ten weeks, the gratitude group felt better about their lives as a whole and more optimistic about the coming week than the hassles group. They also reported fewer physical complaints and spent more time exercising. In further studies, the researchers asked people to write daily, and tested adults with neuromuscular disease, finding similar benefits for mood and sleep.
study.finding: Students who listed blessings each week felt better about their lives and more optimistic than those who listed hassles. They also reported fewer physical complaints and more exercise.

entries.statusNote: Gratitude exercises do seem to help, but less than popular books claim. Meta-analyses (studies pooling many studies), including one by Davis and colleagues in 2016 and another by Cregg and Cheavens in 2021, find small benefits for wellbeing. These often shrink when gratitude is compared with a fair control activity (a neutral task for comparison) rather than listing hassles. Effects on depression and anxiety are small. Some research suggests that writing too often can turn into a chore. The practice is low-risk and may help some people, but it is not a powerful treatment.
life: Try writing three specific good things once or twice a week, rather than every day, so the habit stays fresh.
Write a thank-you letter to someone who helped you and, if you can, read it to them in person.
Do not use gratitude to brush aside real problems; it can sit alongside dealing with them, not replace it.
entries.myth: Gratitude journals are often promoted as a life-changing cure for unhappiness. Careful studies find small average benefits, and they are no substitute for treatment of depression.

quiz.q: Why do critics say some gratitude studies overstate the benefits?
options: Gratitude is harmful
They compare gratitude with listing hassles, which may lower mood
Nobody can feel grateful on purpose
The studies had no participants
quiz.why: Against a neutral activity the benefit is smaller, since listing hassles may make the comparison group feel worse.

entries.title: Social connection and health
entries.line: People with strong social ties live longer, on average, than isolated people, an effect comparable to well-known health risks.
entries.idea: Humans are social animals, and our bodies seem to know it. People with close relationships, regular contact and a sense of belonging tend to be healthier and live longer. Isolation (having few contacts) and loneliness (feeling disconnected, even among people) both predict worse health. Several mechanisms may be at work. Friends and family encourage healthy habits and help in a crisis. Long-term loneliness keeps the body's stress systems switched on, which can affect blood pressure, sleep and inflammation. And social bonds give life meaning, which supports motivation and mental health. The causation runs both ways, though: illness can also shrink a person's social world, which makes the evidence tricky to untangle.

study.name: The Alameda County study
study.ref: Berkman, L. F., & Syme, S. L. (1979). Social networks, host resistance, and mortality: A nine-year follow-up study of Alameda County residents. American Journal of Epidemiology, 109(2), 186-204.
study.story: In 1965 researchers surveyed a large random sample of adults living in Alameda County, California, the area around Oakland and Berkeley. Nearly seven thousand people answered questions about their lives: whether they were married, how many close friends and relatives they had and how often they saw them, whether they belonged to a church, and whether they took part in clubs or other groups. They also answered questions about their health and habits, such as smoking, drinking, exercise and weight. Nine years later the epidemiologists Lisa Berkman and Leonard Syme checked who had died, using death records. They combined the different kinds of social ties into a single network score, running from the most isolated to the most connected. The pattern was striking. Across age groups, people with the fewest social ties were much more likely to have died during those nine years than people with the most, roughly two to three times as likely, depending on sex. Importantly, the link held after taking into account people's health at the start of the study, their income and habits like smoking, drinking and physical activity. This was one of the first large, careful studies to suggest that social connection itself, not just healthy behaviour, was linked to how long people live.
study.finding: Over nine years, the most isolated people died at roughly two to three times the rate of the most connected. This held even after accounting for health habits and earlier health.

entries.statusNote: The association is robust. A 2010 meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) by Julianne Holt-Lunstad and colleagues, combining about 150 studies and over 300,000 people, found that stronger social relationships went with roughly 50 per cent higher odds of survival over the study periods. Large later studies agree. The hard part is causation: these are observational studies, and hidden factors such as early illness or personality could explain some of the link. Comparisons with smoking are rough. Still, the evidence is strong enough that health bodies now treat isolation as a public health issue.
life: Treat regular contact with friends like exercise: schedule it, because it matters for long-term health.
Check in on older neighbours or relatives who live alone; a short weekly call can mean a lot to them.
Loneliness in a crowd counts too; aim for a few close, trusting relationships, not just many contacts.
entries.myth: A popular line says loneliness is exactly as deadly as smoking fifteen cigarettes a day. That comparison is a loose summary of mortality statistics, not a precise measure, but the underlying link is real.

quiz.q: Why is it hard to prove that social isolation itself shortens life?
options: The studies are too small
Illness and other hidden factors can cause both isolation and early death
Nobody has studied it
Isolated people refuse to take part in surveys
quiz.why: In observational studies, a third factor like poor health may lead to both fewer contacts and earlier death.

entries.title: Locus of control
entries.aka: Internal versus external control; perceived control
entries.line: People differ in how far they believe their actions shape their outcomes, and a sense of control goes with wellbeing.
entries.idea: Julian Rotter introduced locus of control in the 1950s and 1960s. People with an internal locus tend to believe that what happens to them depends mainly on their own effort and choices. People with an external locus tend to see outcomes as driven by luck, fate or powerful others. Most people sit somewhere in between, and the balance can differ between areas of life, such as health and work. An internal locus is linked with more effort, better health habits, higher job satisfaction and lower stress. But realism matters: some things genuinely are outside our control, and blaming yourself for them can backfire. Closely related ideas include self-efficacy, which is confidence that you can do a specific task, and learned helplessness.

study.name: The nursing home plant study
study.ref: Langer, E. J., & Rodin, J. (1976). The effects of choice and enhanced personal responsibility for the aged: A field experiment in an institutional setting. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 34(2), 191-198.
study.story: In 1976 Ellen Langer and Judith Rodin ran a study in a nursing home in Connecticut that became one of psychology's most quoted stories. Residents on two floors were similar in health and background. On one floor, the home's administrator gave a talk stressing that residents were responsible for themselves: they could decide how to arrange their rooms, how to spend their time and whom to visit. Each resident was offered a plant to choose and look after, and could choose which night to watch a film. On the other floor, the administrator gave an equally friendly talk stressing that the staff were there to care for them. These residents were each handed a plant that the nurses would water, and were told which night they would see the film. Three weeks later, residents on the responsibility floor were rated by nurses, who did not know the plan, as more alert and active, and they described themselves as happier. They also took part more in activities, such as a contest to guess the number of jelly beans in a jar. When Rodin and Langer returned about eighteen months later, they reported that fewer residents from the responsibility floor had died. The idea that a small dose of control could lengthen life captured the public imagination.
study.finding: Residents encouraged to make choices became more active and happier than those told staff would care for them. A small follow-up also reported fewer deaths.

entries.statusNote: Measures of locus of control and related beliefs reliably predict outcomes such as job satisfaction, health behaviour and stress. But the links are moderate and partly overlap with other traits. The nursing home study is a different matter. It was small, the death figures rested on a handful of cases, and it has not been convincingly replicated (repeated with the same result). A related study by Richard Schulz found that the benefits of control faded, and even reversed, once the control was taken away. A sense of control matters, but the famous life-saving plant is weak evidence.
life: When you feel stuck, list which parts of the problem you can influence and start there, rather than dwelling on what you cannot.
When caring for older relatives or children, offer real choices, even small ones, instead of doing everything for them.
Avoid blaming yourself for genuinely outside events; an internal locus works best when it is realistic.
entries.myth: The nursing home plant study is often told as proof that a sense of control makes people live longer. The finding was small and has not been convincingly replicated, so treat it as a hint, not a fact.

quiz.q: What later finding complicated the idea that giving people control always helps?
options: Control never matters to wellbeing
When control was given and then taken away, people could end up worse off
Only young people benefit from control
Plants make residents unhappy
quiz.why: Schulz found that benefits faded and even reversed once the control ended, so lasting control seems to matter.

entries.title: The impostor phenomenon
entries.line: Many capable people feel like frauds who will be found out, crediting their success to luck rather than ability.
entries.idea: The impostor phenomenon is the persistent feeling that you are not as competent as others think, and that your success comes from luck, charm or other people's mistakes rather than ability. People who experience it often dread being found out, overprepare for every task or put tasks off, and brush aside praise. Each success brings brief relief and then renewed worry, because it was 'just luck again'. The feelings are common among high achievers, students in demanding courses, and people who are new to a role or feel they do not fit in. It is not an official mental health diagnosis, and it overlaps with anxiety, perfectionism and low self-esteem. The popular term 'syndrome' is misleading.

study.name: The impostor phenomenon in high-achieving women
study.ref: Clance, P. R., & Imes, S. A. (1978). The imposter phenomenon in high achieving women: Dynamics and therapeutic intervention. Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice, 15(3), 241-247.
study.story: In the 1970s the psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, working at Georgia State University, began noticing a surprising pattern among their clients and students. Many of the women they saw were outstanding by any outside measure. They had doctorates, top exam results, academic honours and respected jobs. Yet in therapy sessions and conversations they described a quiet, persistent fear. They felt they were not truly intelligent and had somehow fooled everyone around them. Some academics believed they had been hired by mistake. Some students with excellent grades believed an admissions committee had slipped up. Success did not reassure them; it only raised the stakes for the moment when they would finally be exposed. Clance and Imes drew on their work with more than 150 such women over several years, and in 1978 they published a paper giving the experience a name: the impostor phenomenon. They described the cycle that kept it going: worry, then hard work or overpreparation, then success, a brief sense of relief, and finally the conclusion that the success had been a fluke. They suggested that family dynamics and gender stereotypes helped feed it, and described group therapy techniques to challenge it. The paper was based on clinical observation rather than a controlled study, but it struck a chord far beyond the therapy room.
study.finding: Many high-achieving women put their success down to luck or error rather than ability. They feared being exposed as frauds, despite clear evidence of their competence.

entries.statusNote: The experience is real and common, but the science is untidy. In 2020, Dena Bravata and colleagues published a systematic review (a careful survey of all relevant studies). Reported rates ranged from under a tenth to over three quarters of the people studied. They depended on the measure and the group, which shows how inconsistent the measures are. Contrary to the original framing, many studies find men report it too, with small or mixed gender differences. It overlaps heavily with anxiety and perfectionism, and treatment studies are few. It is useful as a description, but weak as a precise concept.
life: Keep a simple record of your achievements and the feedback you receive, and read it when the fraud feeling strikes.
Talk about it: hearing respected colleagues admit the same feelings often loosens their grip.
Watch for overpreparation and brushing off praise; ask whether the extra hours serve the work or just soothe fear.
entries.myth: Popular articles often claim that most people have impostor syndrome and that it mainly affects women. Estimates vary enormously with the measure used, and men report it too.

quiz.q: Why do estimates of how common the impostor phenomenon is vary so widely?
options: Because it only exists in some countries
Because studies use different measures and cut-offs
Because it is a rare medical condition
Because only women have ever been studied
quiz.why: Without an agreed measure or threshold, prevalence figures depend heavily on how each study defines it.

entries.title: Fast and slow thinking
entries.line: Much thinking is fast, automatic and intuitive, while slower, effortful reasoning can check it, but often does not.
entries.idea: Dual-process theories divide thinking into two broad modes. One is fast, automatic, effortless and intuitive: recognising a face, reading a word, sensing that a deal seems too good to be true. Daniel Kahneman, borrowing terms from Keith Stanovich and Richard West, called it System 1. The other, System 2, is slow, deliberate and effortful: working out 17 times 24, comparing mortgage offers, checking an argument. Most of the time System 1 runs the show and does well. But it relies on shortcuts that can lead us astray, and System 2 is lazy, often accepting the first answer that comes to mind. Many biases in this encyclopedia, such as anchoring and the availability heuristic, are described as intuitive errors that slower thinking failed to catch.

study.name: The Cognitive Reflection Test
study.ref: Frederick, S. (2005). Cognitive reflection and decision making. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 19(4), 25-42.
study.story: Try this. A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs one dollar more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? For most people, an answer leaps to mind at once: ten cents. It feels obviously right. It is wrong. If the ball cost ten cents, the bat would cost $1.10, and together they would cost $1.20. The correct answer is five cents. In 2005 Shane Frederick, then at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, published a three-question test built around puzzles like this one, which he called the Cognitive Reflection Test. Each question has a tempting wrong answer that pops into mind and a correct answer that needs a pause to check. Another asks how long 100 machines would take to make 100 widgets, if five machines take five minutes to make five widgets. The tempting answer is 100 minutes; the right one is five. Frederick gave the test to more than 3,000 people, mostly students at universities across the United States, ranging from elite institutions such as MIT and Princeton to large state universities. Many people got most or all of the questions wrong, even at top universities, and most wrong answers were the tempting intuitive ones. People who scored higher also tended to be more patient in choices about money.
study.finding: Many respondents, even at elite universities, gave the intuitive wrong answers, and higher scorers made more patient choices about money.

entries.statusNote: The Cognitive Reflection Test findings replicate well (other researchers get the same results). The broad distinction between quick intuition and deliberate thought is useful and widely accepted. But the idea of two separate systems in the mind is contested. Many researchers see a continuum, and some argue the two-way split is too tidy. Several striking examples in Kahneman's 2011 bestseller Thinking, Fast and Slow also came from priming studies that later failed to replicate, as Kahneman himself acknowledged. The core idea stands; some of its famous illustrations do not.
life: For important decisions, sleep on it or write out your reasoning; slowing down gives deliberate thinking a chance to check intuition.
When an answer to a tricky question feels instantly obvious, take a second look; that is when the bat-and-ball trap bites.
Trust well-trained intuition in familiar areas, like an experienced driver's, but be wary of gut feelings in unfamiliar ones.
entries.myth: Many people picture System 1 and System 2 as two separate parts of the brain, with intuition always the villain. They are useful labels for kinds of thinking, and intuition is often accurate, especially with expertise.

quiz.q: What makes a Cognitive Reflection Test question tricky?
options: It requires advanced maths
It has a tempting intuitive answer that is wrong
It has no correct answer
It tests general knowledge
quiz.why: The questions are easy to solve with a moment's checking, but an attractive wrong answer springs to mind first.
